Commenters stated that the INA creates a statutory right to “meaningful” administrative review before the Board, citing for example, to sections 101(a)(47)(B), 240(c)(4)(C) and (c)(5), and 292 of the Act, 8 U.S.C. 1101(a)(47)(B), 1229a(c)(4)(C) and (c)(5), and 1362, as well as Supreme Court precedent such as DHS v. Thuraissigiam, 591 U.S. 103 (2020), and Garland v. Ming Dai, 593 U.S. 357 (2021). Commenters claimed that the IFR’s summary dismissal procedures violate this statutory right to appeal by treating such appeals as discretionary, with many appeals likely to be summarily dismissed without any review.

Further, some commenters claimed that certain INA provisions also provide for baseline procedural requirements. For example, commenters pointed to language in section 101(a)(47)(B) of the Act, 8 U.S.C. 1101(a)(47)(B), referencing a “determination” by the Board “affirming” an order as requiring a substantive review and decision on each appeal. Similarly, commenters argued that the statutory right to counsel “in any appeal proceedings before the Attorney General” in section 292 of the Act, 8 U.S.C. 1362, and the rebuttable presumption of credibility “on appeal” in section 240(c)(4)(C) of the Act, 8 U.S.C. 1229a(c)(4)(C), would be rendered superfluous if the Board did not conduct a substantive review in each case. Also, commenters asserted, Congress would not have set such a significant Board appeal filing fee in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act20 if appeals were going to be summarily dismissed as the default.

Commenters further stated that the IFR’s summary dismissal procedures are contrary to the INA’s exhaustion requirements in section 242(d)(1) of the Act, 8 U.S.C. 1252(d)(1), because the summary dismissal procedures make the Board’s administrative appeal process discretionary, which conflicts with the exhaustion statute’s references to exhausting all administrative “remedies” that are available to the alien “as of right.” Citing Santos-Zacaria v. Garland, 598 U.S. 411 (2023), commenters explained that this statutory language provides an administrative remedy through the Board appeal process as a matter of right, and they argued that the IFR’s summary dismissal procedures violate this right by treating appeals as discretionary by default, thereby preventing aliens from 20 See generally One Big Beautiful Bill Act, Pub. L. 119–21, sec. 100013(d)–(e), 139 Stat. 72 (2025). receiving meaningful review of their claims. Commenters further argued that to hold otherwise would render section 242(d)(1) of the Act, 8 U.S.C. 1252(d)(1), superfluous, as there are no other administrative remedies available under the INA for aliens in removal proceedings to exhaust other than a Board appeal.

Response: The Department disagrees with commenters that the IFR’s summary dismissal procedures violate the INA. As an initial matter, commenters mischaracterize the appellate process contained in the rule as discretionary; it is not. The rule still allows an alien to file an appeal and requires the Board to review the appeal. It does not authorize the Board to reject an appeal out of hand without review, as a matter of discretion or otherwise. This mischaracterization compounds commenters’ confusion of an alien’s ability to file an appeal—which the rule does not alter—with an alien’s alleged entitlement to a non-summary decision by the Board, which is not located in any text of the INA. Assuming there is a statutory right to an appeal to the Board located in the INA,21 this rule does not alter that right. In other words, this rule’s summary dismissal procedures do not address an alien’s ability to file an appeal; rather, the rule modifies the Board’s procedures after such an appeal has been filed.

Further, as some commenters acknowledged, the INA does not contain any explicit references to—let alone mandates for—specific Board procedures. Rather, the statute contains one explicit reference to the Board, see INA 101(a)(47)(B), 8 U.S.C. 1101(a)(47)(B), and a handful of cursory references to “appeals” or “administrative appeals,” see, e.g., INA 208(d)(5)(A)(iii)–(iv), 8 U.S.C. 1158(d)(5)(A)(iii)–(iv); INA 238(a)(3)(A), 8 U.S.C. 1228(a)(3)(A); INA 240(c)(5), 8 U.S.C. 1229a(c)(5); INA 292, 8 U.S.C. 1362.

21 The Department does not concede such a statutory right exists. But even if it does, “[b]ased on the fact that [8 U.S.C. 1101(a)(47)(B)] contains the only mention of the BIA in the INA, it seems clear that Congress has left all procedural aspects of the BIA, especially how it hears cases, entirely to the Attorney General’s discretion.” Dia, 353 F.3d at 237.

Most importantly, far from creating a detailed statutory framework for administrative appeals, these provisions are silent as to the form or structure of such appeals. Indeed, Congress could have—and can at any time—provide for specific procedures for administrative appeals, just as Congress provided extensive procedures for removal proceedings before Immigration Judges. See INA 240, 8 U.S.C. 1229a et seq. But Congress has not done so. Rather, to the extent the statute creates any right to an administrative appeal, Congress has remained silent as to the procedures for adjudicating any such appeals; those procedures are thus left to the Attorney General to prescribe by regulation. See HSA 1102, 116 Stat. at 2273–74; INA 103(g)(2), 8 U.S.C. 1103(g)(2); see also Dia, 353 F.3d at 237; Blanco de Belbruno v. Ashcroft, 362 F.3d 272, 280 (4th Cir. 2004) (“One section of the INA refers to the existence of the BIA . . . and other sections refer to an administrative appeal for asylum seekers . . . . But the INA is simply silent as to what procedures should apply to that appeal . . . . This fact suggests that the INA vests broad discretion in the Attorney General to fashion the procedures of the BIA.”).

So long as such procedures are constitutionally permissible and such regulations comply with the APA—as the Department believes the IFR and this final rule are and do—the Attorney General has the full authority to modify such procedures by regulation to address problems as they arise. See Zhang v. Dep’t of Justice, 362 F.3d 155, 157 (2d Cir. 2004); Blanco, 362 F.3d at 280; see also Vt. Yankee Nuclear Power Corp. v. Nat. Res. Def. Council, Inc., 435 U.S. 519, 524 (1978) (“Even apart from the Administrative Procedure Act this Court has for more than four decades emphasized that the formulation of procedures was basically to be left within the discretion of the agencies to which Congress had confided the responsibility for substantive judgments.”).

Under the Attorney General’s authority, the Department has carefully reviewed Board processes in an attempt to address critical backlogs at the Board, just as it did over 25 years ago in its past streamlining efforts, see, e.g., Executive Office for Immigration Review; Board of Immigration Appeals; Streamlining, 64 FR 56135, 56137–38 (Oct. 18, 1999), and attempted to further address in 2020, see Appellate Procedures and Decisional Finality in Immigration Proceedings; Administrative Closure, 85 FR 81588 (Dec. 16, 2020). Recognizing that past streamlining efforts, while beneficial, have not kept pace with unprecedented appeal numbers, the Department understood that dramatic changes were necessary. See 91 FR 5268–70. Those changes include, as relevant here, shifting the administrative appellate process to expand the use of summary dismissal to allow the Board to focus its resources on issuing written opinions in cases presenting novel or complex legal issues. The Department believes that this summary dismissal change will create significant efficiencies and make a meaningful difference in addressing the Board’s lengthy backlog.

Additionally, the Department disagrees that any of the statutory references or cases cited by commenters create any specific procedural requirements before the Board. Some commenters pointed to references in section 101(a)(47)(B) of the Act, 8 U.S.C. 1101(a)(47)(B), to a “determination” by the Board “affirming” an order as creating requirements for the Board to review each appeal and issue a substantive opinion. However, commenters read too much into this language, and that argument has been rejected by Federal courts previously during litigation over prior regulations streamlining Board procedures. See, e.g., Dia, 353 F.3d at 237 (explaining that section 101(a)(47)(B) “says absolutely nothing about procedures to be employed by the BIA, or the right to, or manner of, review generally”). This definitional language simply explains when an order of deportation is final, which is when a Board’s order is issued or, if no appeal is taken, when the appeal period ends. In no way does this language convey any substantive requirements for what such a Board order must contain, much less the procedures by which the Board must issue an order. Atemnkeng v. Barr, 948 F.3d 231, 239 (4th Cir. 2020); Blanco, 362 F.3d at 280; Dia, 353 F.3d at 237.

Furthermore, this rule is consistent with the INA’s language. Under this rule’s summary dismissal procedures, if the Board does not vote en banc to accept an appeal for full briefing and further review, the Board will dismiss the appeal without opinion by issuing an order summarily dismissing the alien’s appeal. However, in no way does that suggest that the Board did not review the appeal; instead, it simply means the Board did not find it worthy of further consideration. See 8 CFR 1003.1(d)(2)(ii).

Commenters’ references to other sections of the INA are similarly misplaced. The ability to retain counsel during the Board appeals process, INA 292, 8 U.S.C. 1362, or to maintain a rebuttable presumption of credibility on appeal, INA 208(b)(1)(B)(iii), 8 U.S.C. 1158(b)(1)(B)(iii), are discrete provisions that provide exactly what they state— no more, no less. Neither provision is affected by the IFR’s summary dismissal procedures; aliens continue to have the statutory right to counsel during the Board appeals process, as well as a rebuttable presumption of credibility during the appeals process, when applicable.

Similarly, commenters argued that the INA’s exhaustion statute for Federal court review in section 242(d)(1) of the Act, 8 U.S.C. 1252(d)(1), requires aliens to exhaust administrative remedies available “as of right,” which in turn requires Board appeals to be treated as a legal entitlement with no discretion to deny review under Santos-Zacaria, 598 U.S. at 424–26. However, as explained in the IFR, the Department drafted the IFR with the intention that the rule “would not change any existing understandings regarding when a removal order becomes final or when a petition for review must be filed.” See 91 FR 5271. Put differently, nothing about the rule affects section 242(d)(1) of the Act, 8 U.S.C. 1252(d)(1), because the rule does not affect an alien’s ability to seek review by the Board.

In sum, “[a]bsent constitutional constraints or extremely compelling circumstances, the administrative agencies should be free to fashion their own rules of procedure and to pursue methods of inquiry capable of permitting them to discharge their multitudinous duties.” Vt. Yankee Nuclear Power Corp., 435 U.S. at 543 (internal quotations omitted). That is all the Department has done here.

c. Additional Concerns with Summary Dismissal Commenters raised a number of additional miscellaneous concerns regarding the IFR’s summary dismissal procedures. The Department acknowledges the comments and has thoroughly considered them; however, none is persuasive, and the criticisms in them are vastly outweighed by the efficiency benefits that the rule would provide. Comment: Commenters stated that summarily dismissing most appeals will allow erroneous legal decisions by Immigration Judges to stand, thereby undermining EOIR’s mission to adjudicate immigration cases by fairly and uniformly interpreting immigration laws, as well as likely leading to erroneous removals.

Response: If an alien’s appeal to the Board is summarily dismissed, the alien may raise any alleged legal errors made by the agency before the Federal circuit courts for further review, except where Congress has expressly stated that Federal court review is not available. Additionally, the alien may file a motion to reconsider before the Immigration Court or the Board, as applicable. Under the current procedures, there is also a risk of erroneous decisions by Immigration Judges being affirmed by the Board.22 Because the Board will still review each appeal, however, the rule does not alter the possibility of the Board making an erroneous decision. Moreover, as is the case now, erroneous decisions by the Board will still be subject to correction by Federal courts. Comment: Commenters similarly noted that summary dismissal will functionally 22 Indeed, legal error is inherent in any system of adjudication and is impossible to eliminate—even by an appeals court. C.f. Brown v. Allen, 344 U.S. 443, 427 (1953) (Jackson, J., concurring) (“There is no doubt that if there were a super-Supreme Court, a substantial proportion of our reversals of state courts would also be reversed. We are not final because we are infallible, but we are infallible only because we are final.”).

exhaust all appeal options for most types of claims for discretionary immigration relief. Response: This point describes the situation currently, which is unchanged by the rule. Once the Board rules on an appeal regarding a discretionary form of relief other than asylum, there is limited recourse to Federal court. The rule does not alter that dynamic.

Comment: Commenters argued that Federal court review is not sufficient, as Federal courts have narrower jurisdiction and use more deferential standards of review than the Board, and that PFRs serve a fundamentally different purpose: to review the appellate determinations made by the Board.

Response: The scope of Federal court review, including comments related to jurisdiction and applicable standards of review, is outside the scope of the rule, and the Department declines to predict how Federal courts will interpret the provisions of the rule. The Department emphasizes, however, that this rule does not change any procedures related to seeking Federal court review or existing substantive standards that constrain Federal court jurisdiction.

Nothing in this rule affects the baseline process of filing a PFR to allege errors in the underlying proceedings. Immigration Judges will continue to issue decisions in removal proceedings, which may then be addressed by the Board through a summary dismissal order or an adjudication with briefing. Regardless of how the Board chooses to handle a specific appeal, the alien will then maintain the existing ability to further file a PFR of that decision with the relevant Federal court, which will accept briefing and provide further review of the alleged issues according to existing procedures. See, e.g., INA 242(b), 8 U.S.C. 1252(b) (providing requirements and standards for PFRs). With regard to the alleged limitations of Federal court review, the Department notes that Congress explicitly exempted from review denials of certain discretionary forms of relief and factual issues when the alien is removable on certain criminal grounds. See INA 242(a)(2)(B)–(D); 8 U.S.C. 1252(a)(2)(B)–(D). If Congress wished to provide specific procedures for administrative review of such claims in lieu of or in addition to Federal court review, or to provide certain standards of review for any administrative appeals, it could certainly do so; but it has not. Instead, Congress chose to explicitly limit Federal court review while leaving any administrative appellate processes and standards to the Attorney General. See, e.g., Dia, 353 F.3d at 237 (“[I]t seems clear that Congress has left all procedural aspects of the BIA, especially how it hears cases, entirely to the Attorney General’s discretion.”). As a result, in implementing this rule’s summary dismissal procedures, the Department balanced any limitations on the availability of Federal court review, among other concerns, with the strong need to address the Board’s growing backlog of overwhelmingly straightforward cases. See 91 FR 5271.

In doing so, the Department also notes that, in addition to PFRs in the Federal courts, Congress explicitly provided aliens with a statutory right to file a motion to reconsider an Immigration Judge’s removability decision. See INA 240(c)(6), 8 U.S.C. 1229a(c)(6). As the statute clearly states, such motions are intended to address “errors of law or fact in the previous order . . . .” INA 240(c)(6)(C), 8 U.S.C. 1229a(c)(6)(C). Thus, to address the kinds of potential Immigration Judge errors raised by commenters, Congress provided aliens with an additional statutory process for correcting such errors. Comment: Commenters stated that the IFR did not include a timeline for single Board members to refer a case for consideration by the Board en banc. Commenters asserted that this could result in a scenario where a case is automatically dismissed because the timeline to vote to consider an appeal has passed. Commenters also noted that if the Board does not have a quorum, it will be unable to vote to consider an appeal, and all cases would be summarily dismissed until a quorum is available. Commenters worried that meritorious appeals could be summarily dismissed if the Board lacks sufficient members. Alternatively, commenters claimed that without a quorum, DHS would instead refer all potential Board appeals to the Attorney General in lieu of Board review.

Response: The Department is confident that the Board will have no issues establishing a quorum to vote on whether to accept appeals for full briefing and further consideration and thus does not share commenters’ concerns that DHS will make large numbers of referrals directly to the Attorney General to bypass the Board. Further, it is unnecessary to provide specific timelines for single member referrals in this rule, as the Department expects that the Board will implement internal case-processing procedures to ensure compliance with the timelines in this rule.
Comment: Commenters noted that the rule does not contain any standards for determining whether an issue is sufficiently novel or complex to warrant further Board adjudication.
Response: There is no universal standard for determining novelty or complexity, and the Department believes that it is an issue best reserved for the Board to determine on a case-by-case basis.

The Department also clarifies that the rule itself does not explicitly limit the Board to only adjudicating “novel or complex” issues and, as such, has no need to set any such regulatory standards interpreting these terms. See 8 CFR 1003.1(d)(2)(ii)(A) (only requiring a Board vote on whether to accept an appeal for full briefing and further consideration). Rather, the Department expects that the Board will, in its discretion, focus its resources on requesting further briefing and issuing written opinions in appeals presenting novel or complex legal or factual issues, rather than mine-run appeals involving issues sufficiently addressed by the Immigration Judge or controlled by existing Board or Federal court precedent.

Comment: Commenters raised concerns that summary dismissal will occur before briefing, which is where novel or complex legal issues often surface. Commenters also stated that Board members will have to vote whether to accept a case for adjudication without the benefit of a full record or briefing, which will prevent Board members from fully determining the legal and factual issues in the proceedings before the Immigration Judge.

Response: These comments proceeded from erroneous factual premises. First, even under current rules, issues must be raised in the Notice of Appeal—before briefing—or else they will be waived. Thus, if an issue does not surface until briefing, it will be waived anyway, and the Board will not consider it. Consequently, the commenters’ concerns are misplaced.

Second, the Board will have the full record of proceedings from the Immigration Court when it considers the appeal, including the Immigration Judge’s written decision, if applicable, as well as access to the hearing recordings and the Notice of Appeal, which, for purposes of notifying the Board of the legal and factual issues for review, serves a similar function to the appellant’s brief, as it must identify the alleged errors made by the Immigration Judge. Should the Board decide it needs further information and orders briefing, the appellant would expand upon those issues in his or her brief. See Matter of Valencia, 19 I&N Dec. 354, 355 (BIA 1986) (“Depending on the complexity of the issues raised, a brief may be essential to an adequate presentation of the appeal. In all cases, however, the reasons for an appeal must be meaningfully identified on the Notice of Appeal.”).

Novel or complex issues or obvious errors in an Immigration Judge decision can be easily signaled in a Notice of Appeal. For example, underlying criminal convictions often create complex issues in immigration law, but those issues can be succinctly summarized in the Notice of Appeal sufficient to flag for the Board a specific legal issue on which the Board could determine whether to accept the appeal for full briefing and further review. If the Board then voted affirmatively, a briefing schedule would subsequently be issued to fully develop the arguments.
Comment: Commenters stated that summary dismissal would affect cases where administrative review is most necessary, such as appeals filed pro se or under emergency conditions.

Response: The Board will determine whether fulsome review is necessary, and there is no statutory, regulatory, or other legal basis to mandate that all appeals of a particular category automatically receive full review. Moreover, the Department does not believe that there is a policy justification weighing in favor of requiring full briefing of appeals filed by certain classes of aliens. The most efficient use of the Board’s limited resources is to decide appeals involving novel or complex legal or factual situations. Commenters offered no data indicating that the personal characteristics of a specific alien (for example, pro se or detained) make the substantive legal basis of the alien’s appeal any more likely to involve such issues. Thus, rather than treating certain categories of aliens as automatically entitled to further consideration after additional briefing, it is better policy for the Board to consider all appeals equally and determine whether the legal claims themselves merit further consideration.

Comment: Commenters also stated that the rule would favor DHS. For example, because a single Board member would decide whether to refer a case to en banc review solely based on the Notice of Appeal, commenters claimed that aliens will be required to fully frame issues from the outset, but DHS will not have an obligation to fully respond unless the Board orders briefing.

Response: Commenters either misunderstood the rule or were mischaracterizing it, but in either case, the comments proceeded from a false premise. The rule does not favor either party. DHS has the same obligations as an alien when it is the party filing the appeal, and the alien is in the same position as DHS when an alien files an appeal. The rule does not provide DHS with any special treatment. The Board’s decision to accept a case for full briefing and further review will be based solely on the Board’s determination that the case would benefit from further review, and not who the filing party is. Moreover, if a case is accepted for full briefing and further review, both parties will have the ability to file briefs explaining their position on the relevant issues on appeal. These comments are misplaced.

Comment: Relatedly, commenters expressed concerns that aliens would not have an opportunity to file a written response to DHS-filed Notices of Appeal before the Board decides whether to accept the appeal. Specifically, commenters were concerned that this would give DHS disproportionate power to frame issues in such a way that the Board will accept their appeals, thereby resulting in decisions that narrow the rights of aliens. Response: Again, these comments mischaracterize the rule. Both parties, regardless of which one is the appellant, are subject to the same regulations and have the same responsibilities, depending on the procedural posture of the case. And the parties will have an opportunity to submit briefs in most cases not summarily dismissed by the Board,23 so no decision will result from such appeals without the alien having an opportunity to respond to the issues raised in DHS’s Notice of Appeal, an aspect of the process that commenters failed to acknowledge.

Comment: Commenters also argued that the recently increased filing fee for appeals is exceedingly high for appeals that, in a majority of cases, would be summarily dismissed by the Board, and that the Department should therefore reduce or eliminate the fee. Relatedly, commenters claimed that restrictions on fee waivers would make such waivers largely unavailable, citing the Board’s recent decision in Matter of Garcia Martinez, 29 I&N Dec. 169 (BIA 2025).

23 The Board’s longstanding practice has been to not issue a separate briefing schedule for most interlocutory appeals, though the party against whom such an appeal is sought may always file an opposition to the appeal.

Response: Comments on Department fees are beyond the scope of this rulemaking; however, the Department has fully considered the impact of the increased fees—as well as the continued availability of fee waivers—in promulgating this rule and has determined that such an impact on aliens does not outweigh the beneficial effects of the rule. See 91 FR 5270 n.10. The Department notes that Congress—not the Department—recently increased the appeal filing fee before the Board. See One Big Beautiful Bill Act, Pub. L. 119-21, sec. 100013(d)–(e), 139 Stat. 72 (2025) (“OBBBA”). As such, the Department has no ability to change this fee. The Department also disagrees with commenters that the increased fee justifies any particular type or amount of administrative review. As explained in the IFR and earlier in this section of this preamble, Congress left Board procedures to the Attorney General to address through regulation, and the Department has determined that the procedures in this rule best address the Board’s overwhelming caseload. See 91 FR 5268.

Moreover, neither OBBBA nor this rule affects the ability of aliens to request fee waivers under existing regulations. See 8 CFR 1003.8(a)(3). The Department disagrees with commenters’ allegations regarding the availability of fee waivers. Although this rule does not make any changes to fee waivers, the Department disagrees with commenters’ characterization of the Board’s decision in Matter of Garcia Martinez, which at base merely explains that aliens requesting a fee waiver must provide sufficient evidence of their inability to pay the requisite filing fee. See 29 I&N Dec. at 171–72. Comment: Commenters further questioned the IFR’s justification that the summary dismissal changes would help offset asymmetry in review available to aliens and DHS. Commenters stated that, if DHS appeals are subject to summary dismissal at the same rate as appeals from aliens, the status quo would remain the same, with one more level of review available to aliens than DHS.

Commenters raised concerns that the IFR’s summary dismissal procedures will occur before transcripts are produced, which prevents aliens from identifying issues evident in the transcript, including potential due process concerns. As such, commenters stated that aliens will need access to the transcript to survive summary dismissal at the Notice of Appeal stage. Commenters also questioned whether transcripts would be produced for the PFR process before the Federal courts. If so, commenters claimed that any such transcript production could delay Federal court review by months or years. Response: The Department reiterates that the rule applies to both parties. Thus, its requirements apply equally to DHS and an alien, and there is no expectation that one party or the other will benefit from the rule’s changes.

EOIR regulations already provide for several categories of summary dismissals of appeals to the Board without the production of a transcript, see, e.g., 8 CFR 1003.1(d)(2)(A), (C), (F), (G), (H), so the addition of another category does not alter the fundamental structural dynamic.24 Moreover, it has long been the case that issues must be raised in the Notice of Appeal or risk summary dismissal; thus, even under pre-IFR procedures, the parties could not wait until a transcript is produced to raise issues. See 8 CFR 3.3(b) (1997), adopted by Executive Office for Immigration Review; Motions and Appeals in Immigration Proceedings, 61 FR 18900, 18906 (Apr. 29, 1996); 8 CFR 1003.3(b) (2026) (“The party taking the appeal must identify the reasons for the appeal in the Notice of Appeal (Form EOIR-26 or Form EOIR-29) or in any attachments thereto, in order to avoid summary dismissal pursuant to § 1003.1(d)(2)(i).”).

To be clear, the Board does not—and did not prior to this rule—produce transcripts at the Notice of Appeal stage. Rather, aliens filing a Notice of Appeal focus 24 The Board also considers several types of appeals already that do not have transcripts, e.g., appeals of motion to reopen and reconsider decisions, interlocutory appeals, appeals of custody redetermination decisions, and appeals of certain visa decisions by DHS. Commenters failed to acknowledge that these other categories of appeals are processed without any evident concerns even though they do not generate transcripts.

on defects in the Immigration Judge’s decision and, only once an appeal is accepted for full briefing and further review and docketed—and not summarily dismissed under an existing provision—is a transcript of proceedings produced, provided the appeal warrants a transcript in the first instance.25 This rule follows that general understanding: aliens will continue to allege errors in the Immigration Judge’s decision in their Notice of Appeal and, like before, if an alien believes that any errors were the result of testimonial issues necessitating review of the transcripts, he or she can explain this in the Notice of Appeal and the Board will then determine whether such issues warrant further review. To the extent there are concerns about the potential for defective transcripts, those will always exist, regardless of this rule, and can be addressed on a case-by-case basis, as they are now. In short, none of the concerns about transcripts outweigh the efficiency benefits of the rule. Finally, as to commenters’ questions about transcripts during the PFR process, EOIR will produce transcripts for PFRs if needed, and there is no expectation that such production would delay Federal court review by any significant amount of time.
Comment: One commenter expressed confusion over which EOIR determination the Federal courts will review after summary dismissal.

Response: To address the commenter’s confusion over which EOIR determination Federal courts will review, the Department notes this final rule’s changes to 8 CFR 1003.1(d)(2)(ii). The Department is revising 8 CFR 1003.1(d)(2)(ii) to clarify the language the Board will include in a summary dismissal order issued under that paragraph and the effect of such a summary dismissal order for Federal court review. The added language—which is similar to longstanding language applicable in cases where the Board affirms a decision without opinion—clarifies that a summary dismissal 25 For example, a transcript is generally not prepared for interlocutory appeals, appeals of motion to reopen decisions by Immigration Judges, custody redetermination appeals, and appeals of visa petition decisions. order shall be deemed to reflect the same considerations as an order where the Board affirms a decision without opinion: that the result reached in the decision was correct, without necessarily implying approval of all the reasoning; that any errors were harmless or nonmaterial; and that the issues are either squarely controlled by existing Board or Federal court precedent and do not present the application of precedent to a novel factual situation or the factual and legal issues raised on appeal are not so substantial to warrant a written opinion. See 8 CFR 1003.1(d)(2)(ii)(C).

Comment: Commenters provided recommendations related to the summary dismissal provisions, asserting that the recommendations would improve transparency and preserve core adjudicatory functions while aligning with the Department’s efficiency goal. Commenters suggested establishing criteria to guide the selection of cases for review with briefing, stating that while discretion is essential, the lack of any established criteria could lead to inconsistency. Commenters stated that regular sampling and assessment would allow the agency to refine its selection process.

Response: The Department considered adopting regulatory criteria to guide the Board’s consideration whether to summarily dismiss appeals but ultimately determined that the Board is best suited to adopt internal procedures and criteria for selecting cases where further briefing is necessary for review. The Department agrees that regular auditing of internal procedures is useful to ensure the success of the program; however, codifying such a program through rulemaking is unnecessary, as the Department already has such standard management practices. See, e.g., 8 CFR 1003.1(e) (“The Chief Appellate Immigration Judge, under the supervision of the Director, shall be responsible for the success of the case management system.”).
Comment: Commenters expressed concern that an appellate framework that consists of a Notice of Appeal followed by summary dismissal may incentivize unscrupulous attorneys to perform substandard work.

Response: The Department does not share commenters’ concerns that the provisions of this rule will incentivize any attorneys to perform substandard work, as all practitioners appearing before the Immigration Courts and the Board remain subject to EOIR’s professional conduct regulations. See, e.g., 8 CFR 1003.101 et seq. Further, State bars may always analyze and address, or decline to address, a practitioner’s conduct, including any alleged substandard work, according to their own rules if the practitioner is an attorney subject to their disciplinary authority.

2. 10-day Appeal Deadline a. Due Process Concerns Comment: Numerous commenters asserted that by shortening the appeal deadline from 30 days to 10 days, the IFR deprives aliens of their constitutional guarantee of a full and fair hearing under the Due Process Clause of the Fifth Amendment by severely restricting their right to representation by counsel and a meaningful opportunity to be heard. Commenters asserted these impacts would be particularly acute in cases of detained aliens, pro se aliens, and unaccompanied alien children (“UACs”).

Commenters also argued that the 10-day appeal deadline imposed by the IFR deprives aliens of due process by creating another procedural barrier to meaningful review, as 10 days, according to commenters, is an insufficient amount of time for an alien to either apply for a fee waiver or to gather funds to pay the substantial filing fee for appeals. Commenters stated that other appellate tribunals provide longer deadlines to file appeals.

Response: The Department disagrees with commenters’ assertion that the 10-day appeal deadline deprives aliens of due process by restricting their right to be represented by counsel or to a meaningful opportunity to be heard.

To begin, commenters misconstrued an alien’s right to counsel in immigration proceedings and the alleged due process implications. Under the Fifth Amendment, aliens are guaranteed due process in immigration proceedings, see Reno v. Flores, 507 U.S. 292, 306 (1993), but the Sixth Amendment’s right to counsel applies only to “criminal prosecutions,” U.S. Const. amend. VI. Notably, Congress has provided aliens with substantial due process protections by statute, including the “privilege of being represented, at no expense to the Government, by counsel of the alien’s choosing who is authorized to practice in [] [immigration] proceedings” including “any appeal proceedings before the Attorney General from any such removal proceedings.” INA 240(b)(4)(A), 292, 8 U.S.C. 1229a(b)(4)(A), 1362.

But importantly, an alien’s failure to obtain counsel in immigration proceedings does not constitute a due process violation. See Vides-Vides v. INS, 783 F.2d 1463, 1470 (9th Cir. 1986). The IFR focuses entirely on the appellate process before the Board and does not address or affect an alien’s statutory privilege of being represented by counsel of the alien’s choosing, at no expense to the Government, regardless of whether initially placed into removal proceedings or at any other point in time during the pendency of the case. See INA 240(b)(4)(A), 292, 8 U.S.C. 1229a(b)(4)(A), 1362. Moreover, the IFR’s 10-day appeal deadline aligns with the existing 10-day statutory timeframe aliens are afforded to find counsel prior to the initial immigration hearing after the commencement of immigration proceedings. INA 239(b)(1), 8 U.S.C. 1229(b)(1). If that timeline is sufficient to find counsel for the initial hearing, it is unclear why it would not also be sufficient for an appeal. See generally Dakane v. Att’y Gen., 399 F.3d 1269, 1273 n.6 (11th Cir. 2005) (“[T]he Supreme Court has held that [aliens] are ensured a fundamentally fair hearing through statutory protections provided for by Congress”). Commenters also artificially limited their due process arguments to the narrow Board appeal window, rather than acknowledging that Board appeals are only part of an often-lengthy administrative process before EOIR. Aliens placed in proceedings before an Immigration Judge are advised of their right to self-funded counsel and are often provided continuances to find counsel. See, e.g., 8 CFR 1240.10(a)(1). Removal proceedings then proceed to determine removability and adjudicate any potential applications for relief or protection. Only once an Immigration Judge issues a decision does the appeal period begin to run. Throughout this entire process, aliens have the ability to retain counsel. So, arguing that the 10-day appeal period after the conclusion of removal proceedings is the only relevant period to consider due process concerns misrepresents the actual, lengthy process of such cases. Being given a reasonable amount of time to obtain counsel in a proceeding where counsel is not guaranteed does not rise to the level of a due process violation. Thus, the Department finds commenters’ allegations that the IFR’s 10-day appeal deadline deprives aliens of due process by restricting their right to counsel are without merit.

The Department similarly finds meritless commenters’ assertion that the IFR’s 10-day appeal deadline undermines due process by imposing procedural barriers that deprive aliens of a meaningful opportunity to be heard. The Department stresses that the IFR’s 10-day appeal deadline does not prevent any class of aliens—e.g., aliens represented by counsel, pro se aliens, detained aliens, or UACs—from seeking an appeal, paying the appeal fee, or applying for a fee waiver. The procedures for filing an appeal, just as they existed before the IFR, simply require aliens to complete the appeal form by providing, with specificity, the reasons for disagreement with the Immigration Judge’s decision. Similarly, this rule does not change an alien’s ability to apply for a fee waiver, which only requires completion of a simple form listing the alien’s monthly income sources and expense sources. Likewise, even for those aliens who do not qualify for a fee waiver, having to pay the requisite appeal fee should be accounted for throughout their removal proceedings and not come as a surprise.26 None of these requirements—even 26 EOIR notifies aliens that there may be fees associated with any filed appeals in multiple publicly available locations. See, e.g., 8 CFR 1103.7; EOIR, Types of Appeals, Motions, and Required Fees (Feb. 1, under a 10-day appeal period—prevents aliens from having a meaningful opportunity to file a Board appeal. Thus, even if due process required access to an administrative appeal, none of these requirements would violate due process.

Any due process concerns regarding the 10-day deadline are further obviated by the availability of electronic filing and electronic fee payments to EOIR, including the ability of pro se aliens to electronically file the Notice of Appeal with the Board. See generally EOIR, Respondent Access Portal, https://respondentaccess.eoir.justice.gov/en/ [https://perma.cc/7W3Y-JH5R].

Instead, the 10-day appeal deadline treats all classes of aliens equally and serves to expedite the appellate process by allowing aliens to have their appeals reviewed by the Board faster, instead of being delayed as a result of backlogged claims. This will allow aliens to receive expeditious final administrative decisions in their cases and pursue Federal court review faster which, in turn, will aid the Board in addressing its backlog of pending appeals.

Moreover, the IFR’s 10-day appeal deadline only affects the Board’s review process, which is wholly within the authority of the Attorney General. It does not impact any of the procedural protections afforded to aliens in immigration proceedings as set by Congress. See INA 240(b)(4), 8 U.S.C. 1229a(b)(4). The Board is a regulatory creation of the Attorney General; there is no due process or statutory right entitling an alien to an administrative appeal before the Board because the Attorney General has the authority to eliminate the Board entirely and could delegate his power elsewhere. Guentchev, 77 F.3d 2026), https://www.justice.gov/eoir/types-appeals-motions-and-required-fees [https://perma.cc/V8AD- VJDT]; EOIR, EOIR Forms & Fees (Feb. 1, 2026), https://www.justice.gov/eoir/eoir-forms [https://perma.cc/2VX5-KCUE]; EOIR, EOIR Payment Portal, https://epay.eoir.justice.gov/index [https://perma.cc/E8QS-QREY]. Additionally, both the INA and EOIR’s regulations require that Immigration Judges provide aliens with notice about the appeals process. See INA 240(c)(5), 8 U.S.C. 1229a(c)(5) (requiring the Immigration Judge, if ordering an alien removed, to “inform the alien of the right to appeal that decision”); 8 CFR 1240.10(a)(3) (requiring the Immigration Judge to “[a]scertain that the respondent has received a copy of appeal rights”). This ordinarily includes oral and written advisals that a fee may be required for any such appeals.

at 1037 (“Even litigants in the federal courts are not constitutionally entitled to multiple layers of review. The Attorney General could dispense with the Board and delegate her powers to the immigration judges[.]”).

Comment: Commenters also stated that the Ninth Circuit previously determined that a 10-day appeal filing deadline violates the Due Process Clause, citing Gonzales- Julio v. INS, 34 F.3d 820 (9th Cir. 1994). Commenters asserted that in promulgating the IFR, the Department failed to acknowledge that precedent or explain how the IFR’s 10- day deadline does not violate the same constitutional provision.

Response: The Department believes that commenters misunderstood the breadth of the Ninth Circuit’s holding in Gonzales-Julio and, regardless, the circumstances underlying the case have changed over the intervening 30-plus years, such that any due- process concerns raised regarding a 10-day appeal deadline in that case are no longer applicable.27 In Gonzales-Julio, the Ninth Circuit considered the case of an alien who lived in Hawaii and had to file a Notice of Appeal by mail with an office in San Diego, California, within 10 days and concluded that the alien’s due process rights were violated. 34 F.3d at 825. But the facts presented in that case are important. At the time, the ability to electronically file an appeal did not exist; all documents had to be filed with the Office of the Chief Immigration Judge; and filing fees were paid separately to an office of the former Immigration and Naturalization Service. Id. at 822. Further, in cases where an alien sought a fee waiver, “the notice of appeal [wa]s sent directly to the Office and [wa]s not filed until the fee waiver [wa]s approved.” Id. Finally, “no record [wa]s kept of when the notice of appeal [wa]s received, nor [wa]s a notice of appeal date- 27 As noted above, courts have determined that the Due Process Clause does not require an opportunity to file an administrative appeal in immigration proceedings. See, e.g., Dia, 353 F.3d at 242; Guentchev, 77 F.3d at 1037. The Department acknowledges that because the Government has nonetheless granted aliens the right to do so, it cannot impose procedural requirements that unduly restrict that right. See Cleveland Bd. of Educ. v. Loudermill, 470 U.S. 532, 541 (1985). For the reasons explained below, however, this rule’s procedural changes do not impose any problematic burden on the pursuit of administrative appeals from decisions of Immigration Judges.
stamped upon receipt.” Id.

Within the context of these now-outdated appeal procedures, the court concluded that “[w]here a petitioner residing in Hawaii has only ten days to appeal an order of deportation, has no control over the delivery of the mail, and has no control over whether the appeal is filed upon receipt in the Office of the Immigration Judge (especially when a fee waiver is requested),” the alien’s due process rights were violated. Id. at 825. The Ninth Circuit did not hold that a 10-day filing deadline is per se violative of due process rights in all cases and under all circumstances. Moreover, the Ninth Circuit in Gonzales- Julio did not address the possibility of equitable tolling of the filing deadline, which would obviate the concerns raised, and which may be available under this rule. See Matter of Morales-Morales, 28 I&N Dec. 714 (BIA 2023).28 Shortly after the Gonzales-Julio decision, the Eighth Circuit considered a similar challenge from an alien asserting that the 10-day period to file an appeal violated her due process rights. See Talamantes-Penalver v. INS, 51 F.3d 133 (8th Cir. 1995). But the Eighth Circuit held “that the ten-day filing deadline comports with due process, even as applied to aliens living in remote locations who make reasonable efforts to comply with the regulation.” Id. at 135. Seemingly in recognition of the importance of evaluating the facts and circumstances of each individual case, the court explained that “[t]he ten-day filing period arguably could be unconstitutional as applied to a petitioner in Hawaii, a somewhat ‘remote’ location, but constitutional as applied to a petitioner in a location not so remote from the place where the notice of appeal is to be filed.” Id. at 136. In determining that the agency’s procedures provided sufficient due process, the Eighth Circuit emphasized the Government’s “significant” interest in the filing deadline, 28 The Department recognizes that the legal foundation for an administrative agency to exercise equitable authority such as equitable tolling is unclear. Nevertheless, current Board precedent allows for it, and it would mitigate many of the concerns raised by commenters about “one-off” situations in which the new deadline could affect the exercise of a party’s appeal rights.

explaining that filing deadlines aid the Government in “bring[ing] litigation to an end” and “determin[ing] with certainty when an alien’s right to appeal is cut off and the [Immigration Judge]’s deportation order is conclusive.” Id. at 137. And, as remains true today, “[e]nforcement of this nation’s immigration laws is enhanced by the speedy adjudication of cases and the prompt deportation of offenders.” Id.

Accordingly, the Department does not read the Ninth Circuit’s holding in Gonzales-Julio as precluding the adoption of a 10-day appeal deadline in this rule. EOIR has made several changes to its appeal filing procedures since that decision that have alleviated the concerns identified by the Ninth Circuit. Most significantly, the Board implemented electronic filing in 2021 and further expanded electronic filing to allow pro se aliens to file Notices of Appeal with the Board. 91 FR 5272; see also Irigoyen- Briones v. Holder, 644 F.3d 943, 951 (9th Cir. 2011) (“To protect its important interest in proceeding expeditiously with these cases, yet avoid subjecting aliens to the risk of losing their appeals due to bad weather or delivery service error, all the Board need do is what courts and private companies routinely do: allow people to send their notices of appeal over the internet.”). Electronic filing “allows parties to submit Notices of Appeal at any time of day from any location with internet access, removing concerns related to mail delays and the restrictions business hours create to meet filing deadlines.” 91 FR 5272. Similarly, appeal filing fees are also paid directly to the Board via EOIR’s Payment Portal, and regulations clearly establish the Board’s procedure for assessing fee waivers submitted with a Notice of Appeal. See 8 CFR 1003.8(a)(3) (“If the fee waiver request does not establish the inability to pay the required fee, the appeal or motion will not be deemed properly filed, provided the Board grants 15 days to re-file the rejected document with the filing fee or new fee waiver request and tolls any applicable filing deadline during the 15-day cure period.”).

Taken together, the availability of electronic filing for appeals and electronic payments for appeal fees represents a significant shift from the circumstances the Ninth Circuit was considering in Gonzales-Julio, particularly as internet access and usage has become ubiquitous even for pro se aliens. Given the ability to immediately file a Notice of Appeal from any place at any time, the Department believes a 10-day appeal deadline comports with due process. And, even if the specific circumstances presented by an alien’s case could result in the violation of an alien’s due process rights, the Board has the authority to equitably toll the appeal deadline, as discussed above.

b. Statutory Concerns Comment: Commenters stated that a 10-day timeline for appeals violates the INA. Specifically, commenters stated that a 10-day timeline is insufficient for aliens to prepare their claims, including obtaining counsel and obtaining documents that they wish to submit in support of their claims. Commenters asserted that the IFR violates provisions of the INA guaranteeing aliens the right to counsel in removal proceedings, citing sections 240(b)(4) and 292 of the Act, 8 U.S.C. 1229a(b)(4) and 1362. Commenters noted that section 292 of the Act, 8 U.S.C. 1362, specifically provides aliens with a right to counsel “in any appeal proceedings before the Attorney General from any such removal proceedings.” Commenters acknowledged, however, that the INA does not guarantee representation in every case.

Commenters alleged that the IFR’s provisions shortening appeal deadlines will violate this statutory right to counsel by interfering with aliens’ ability to find counsel, particularly if the alien is detained, indigent, or appeared pro se before the Immigration Judge during removal proceedings. Commenters further stated that the shortened appeal deadlines impede counsel’s ability to accept representation in a new case, request the oral record of proceedings, review the case, and prepare an appeal in the allotted time frame, thereby contravening the INA’s right to counsel, which commenters claimed could reduce the availability of competent counsel.

Response: Nothing in the INA precludes the Department from establishing a 10- day deadline to file most appeals with the Board, as is supported by legislative history and prior Departmental policy. Indeed, a 10-day deadline to file an administrative appeal of an Immigration Judge decision is not unprecedented. Notably, after a reorganization consolidated Immigration Judges and the Board into the newly created EOIR, the agency issued a rule establishing “a uniform procedure for filing administrative appeals relating to Immigration Judge proceedings.” Aliens and Nationality; Rules of Procedure for Proceedings Before Immigration Judges, 52 FR 2931 (Jan. 29, 1987). As part of the uniform procedures, the regulatory deadline to file an appeal of a decision of an Immigration Judge was 10 days after service of the decision or 13 days if the decision was mailed. See, e.g., 8 CFR 3.36(b) (1987); 52 FR 2935. These appeal deadlines remained in place for almost a decade, including following Congress’ directive in the Immigration Act of 1990 for the Attorney General to issue regulations with respect to “the time period for the filing of administrative appeals in deportation proceedings.” Pub. L. 101–649, § 545(d), 104 Stat. 4978, 5066 (1990); see also Executive Office for Immigration Review; Rules of Procedures, 57 FR 11568 (Apr. 6, 1992) (amending regulations to implement various provisions of the Immigration Act of 1990 but maintaining existing 10-day appeal deadline); 8 CFR 3.38(b) (1993) (“The notice of appeal of the decision shall be filed with the Office of the Immigration Judge having administrative control over the Record of Proceeding within ten (10) calendar days after service of the decision. Time will be 13 days if mailed.”), 3.1(b) (1993). Subsequently, in passing the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996, Pub. L. 104-208, sec. 604(d)(5)(A)(iv), 110 Stat. 3009–546, 3009–694 (Sept. 30, 1996), Congress enacted a 30-day timeline for filing an appeal for certain asylum-related cases, which overrode the regulatory 10-day period as it applied to such cases. See INA 208(d)(5)(A)(iv), 8 U.S.C. 1158(d)(5)(A)(iv); Liadov v. Mukasey, 518 F.3d 1003, 1009 (8th Cir. 2008) (“Without question, the statute trumped the ten-day appeal period previously adopted in the regulations.”). At the same time, Congress remained silent with respect to timelines for filing appeals from other types of Immigration Judge decisions. Congress’s silence in this regard, against the backdrop of an existing regulatory 10-day filing deadline, indicates that Congress made a determination not to intervene with respect to the 10-day filing deadlines applicable to the other remaining appeal types before the Board.

Nor has Congress taken action since then to codify additional filing deadlines for appeals beyond those specified in section 208(d)(5)(A)(iv) of the Act, 8 U.S.C. 1158(d)(5)(A)(iv). However, DOJ subsequently amended EOIR’s regulations to implement a 30-day filing deadline to appeal from Immigration Judge decisions. See 61 FR 18902. In that rule, DOJ stated that it was increasing the deadline for filing an appeal from 10 to 30 days in order to respond to concerns raised by the Ninth Circuit and commenters regarding the sufficiency of time to initiate the appellate process. However, as already discussed above in this section, circumstances have changed in intervening years, and the Department has therefore determined that a 10-day filing deadline is more appropriate.

The 10-day deadline to file most appeals with the Board is also wholly consistent with the INA’s provisions related to obtaining counsel in Immigration Court proceedings. The INA provides aliens in removal proceedings with “the privilege of being represented, at no expense to the Government, by counsel of the alien’s choosing who is authorized to practice in such proceedings.” INA 240(b)(4)(A), 8 U.S.C. 1229a(b)(4)(A). The INA’s privilege of representation extends to “any appeal proceedings before the Attorney General from any such removal proceedings.” INA 292, 8 U.S.C. 1362. Consistent with the INA’s requirements, EOIR’s regulations clearly state that an alien may be represented in removal proceedings. See 8 CFR 1003.16(b), 1240.3.

Nothing in the IFR nor in this final rule changes any of EOIR’s regulations ensuring that aliens may be represented by counsel of their choosing, at their expense. This rule is focused on streamlining the administrative appellate process, and nothing in this rule prevents, precludes, or limits an alien’s ability to seek counsel. Arguments to the contrary ignore the reality that aliens often have a significant amount of time to seek and obtain counsel prior to their Immigration Court hearing and entry of a removal order, despite the fact that the INA requires aliens be provided only 10 days to seek counsel prior to an initial hearing before an Immigration Judge. See INA 239(b)(1), 8 U.S.C. 1229(b)(1) (“In order that an alien be permitted the opportunity to secure counsel before the first hearing date in proceedings . . . , the hearing date shall not be scheduled earlier than 10 days after the service of the notice to appear, unless the alien requests in writing an earlier hearing date.”).

Moreover, aliens often receive multiple continuances to seek representation before the Immigration Judge. See, e.g., Matter of C-B-, 25 I&N Dec. 888, 889–90 (BIA 2012). Further, an Immigration Judge is required to advise an alien of his or her right to representation, to inquire as to whether the alien desires representation, and to advise the alien about the availability of pro bono legal services. INA 239(a)(1)(E), 8 U.S.C. 1229(a)(1)(E); 8 CFR 1240.10(a)(1)–(2).

Indeed, many aliens are represented in proceedings before an Immigration Judge and may retain the same counsel throughout the appellate process, obviating commenters’ concerns regarding finding and obtaining counsel. The Department also anticipates that, as a potential response to this rule, counsel will likely begin explaining the shortened appeal deadline to clients earlier in removal proceedings and increasing the amount of representation agreements that include administrative appeals as part of the initial agreement.

In cases where an alien is not represented before the Immigration Judge, the Department acknowledges that aliens whose cases are subject to the 10-day appeal period may face difficulties securing representation prior to the deadline for filing a Notice of Appeal with the Board.29 See 91 FR 5272 n.16 (“The Department acknowledges that some aliens proceed pro se before the Immigration Judge and may seek counsel after an adverse decision and that in those circumstances changing the deadline from 30 to 10 days, except for asylum appeals by aliens not barred from applying, may impact their ability to obtain counsel to file a Notice of Appeal.”). However, such aliens likely will have had multiple opportunities to seek and secure counsel prior to the Immigration Judge’s decision, particularly as Immigration Judges generally provide right-to-counsel advisals during the very first hearing in removal proceedings. Functionally, the change in appeal deadline implemented by this rule is 20 fewer days to seek counsel in an often years-long process. And an alien unable to obtain counsel prior to the deadline for filing a Notice of Appeal will also have additional time to continue seeking counsel if the Board accepts the appeal for further consideration with briefing prior to seeking Federal court review.

Difficulties in securing legal representation are not unique to aliens, and many aliens affirmatively elect to forgo legal representation for their own personal reasons. The INA does not guarantee that every alien will obtain legal counsel, nor does it require the Department to delay the efficient completion of removal proceedings beyond the statutorily delineated period of time that an alien must be provided to seek counsel prior to the beginning of removal proceedings before an Immigration Judge. See INA 29 Although the representation rate is higher for appeals before the Board when compared to completed cases before the Immigration Court, it is not clear whether that is due to the nature of cases that are appealed (i.e., a greater percentage of cases with representation file appeals, leading to a higher representation rate at the Board overall) or due to aliens who were unrepresented before the Immigration Courts deciding to obtain representation at the appellate stage. EOIR’s experience is that the former explanation is likely correct, but regardless of the reason, the Department has considered the impact of this final rule on the population of aliens unrepresented at the trial level and ultimately determined that the efficiency benefits of this rule outweigh any potential costs.

239(b)(3), 8 U.S.C. 1229(b)(3) (“Nothing in this subsection may be construed to prevent the Attorney General from proceeding against an alien . . . if the [10-day time period] has elapsed and the alien has failed to secure counsel.”). Had Congress intended to provide another minimum period of time for aliens to seek counsel prior to filing an appeal with the Board, it easily could have done so. Accordingly, this rule’s changes to the appeal deadline do not violate the INA’s requirements.

The Department is further unpersuaded by commenters’ concerns related to counsel’s ability to provide effective legal representation to clients. The Department is unaware of any reason why 10 days is an insufficient amount of time for counsel to file a Notice of Appeal that adequately identifies the issues being raised on appeal. Counsel must only preserve issues in a Notice of Appeal with appropriate specificity; the rule does not require full legal briefing at the Notice of Appeal stage.

Despite commenter assertions to the contrary, the Department considered the impact of the IFR on aliens’ ability to obtain counsel for an appeal to the Board. See 91 FR 5272 n.16. The Department has further considered comments related to legal representation and continues to believe that “the interest in timely adjudications outweighs” potential concerns related to aliens’ ability to obtain counsel and that “the benefits of the reforms in this rule outweigh that potential impact, especially given that such aliens would have had time prior to the removal order to seek the assistance of counsel.” Id. In short, the Department has considered all of the comments and concerns, but it continues to believe that the benefits of the rule outweigh any potential—and highly speculative—costs related to legal representation.

Comment: Commenters argued that the IFR violates section 240(b)(4)(C) of the Act, 8 U.S.C. 1229a(b)(4)(C), which requires EOIR to maintain a complete record of proceedings, and that the 10-day appeal period also conflicts with section 240(c)(6) of the Act, 8 U.S.C. 1229a(c)(6), which provides a 30-day window for motions to reconsider. Response: This rule is wholly consistent with section 240(b)(4)(C) of the Act, 8 U.S.C. 1229a(b)(4)(C), which states that “a complete record shall be kept of all testimony and evidence produced at the proceedings.” Nothing in this rule affects the development of a record in removal proceedings before an Immigration Judge, on which this statutory section focuses. See also 8 CFR 1003.36 (“The Immigration Court shall create and control the Record of Proceeding.”).

Separately, the 10-day appeal filing deadline does not foreclose the statutory availability of motions to reconsider, and any change to the appeal filing deadline is irrelevant to such availability. See INA 240(c)(6), 8 U.S.C. 1229a(c)(6). Nothing in this rule changes the potential avenues for addressing alleged errors in an Immigration Judge’s decision: an alien may choose to file a motion to reconsider with the Immigration Judge, an appeal with the Board, and even a subsequent motion to reconsider following a Board appeal denial. Moreover, should an alien choose to file a motion to reconsider with the Immigration Judge, the alien may appeal any Immigration Judge denial of such motion to the Board and seek further review in the Federal courts if necessary. See, e.g., Form EOIR-26, Notice of Appeal from a Decision of an Immigration Judge, Question 5 (Sept. 2019), https://www.justice.gov/eoir/file/eoir26/dl [https://perma.cc/P3PP-7T3H] (providing an option to file “an appeal from the Immigration Judge’s decision denying a motion to reopen or a motion to reconsider . . . .”) (emphasis in original); Ayala v. Sessions, 855 F.3d 1012, 1020 (9th Cir. 2017) (reviewing Immigration Judge’s denial of motion to reconsider).

Comment: Commenters argued that the IFR violates section 208(d)(5)(A)(iv) of the Act, 8 U.S.C. 1158(d)(5)(A)(iv), which they asserted requires 30 days for an administrative appeal of any decision granting or denying asylum. Commenters argued that the INA does not have a carve-out from the 30-day appeal deadline based on the Immigration Judge’s reasoning in an asylum denial. Further, commenters asserted that the Department’s position in the IFR that asylum seekers whose applications are barred under section 208(a)(2) of the Act, 8 U.S.C. 1158(a)(2), are not entitled to the 30-day appeal deadline has no support in the statute. Commenters expressed that if Congress had intended for there to be a different appeal deadline for asylum applications denied under section 208(a)(2) of the Act, 8 U.S.C. 1158(a)(2), it would have specified it in the INA.

Further, commenters alleged that the Department ignored the second part of section 208(d)(5)(A)(iv) of the Act, 8 U.S.C. 1158(d)(5)(A)(iv), which states that an administrative appeal must be filed within 30 days of a decision granting or denying asylum “or within 30 days of the completion of removal proceedings before an immigration judge under section 240, whichever is later.” Commenters also noted that, functionally, the appeal deadline for nearly all asylum cases will be 10 days because asylum cases almost always include claims for withholding of removal or protection under the regulations implementing the Convention Against Torture and Other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment, Dec. 10, 1984, S. Treaty Doc. No. 100- 20 (1988), 1465 U.N.T.S 85 (“CAT”), and the appeal deadline for those claims remains 10 days.

Commenters also stated that the IFR’s exception for some asylum cases is confusing. Commenters stressed that in order for an alien or the alien’s counsel to know which filing deadline applies, the alien or counsel must understand whether the Immigration Judge denied the asylum application on its merits or on a ground subject to a 10-day appeal deadline. Commenters expressed that it is unclear which deadline applies if an application is denied for multiple reasons, providing as an example an asylum case where an Immigration Judge finds that the one-year bar applies, but also finds that the alien did not demonstrate a well-founded fear of future persecution.

Commenters also stated that although the Department justified the 10-day deadline by asserting it would harmonize administrative appellate deadlines, the Department did not explain how doing the opposite for asylum appeals by implementing two deadlines contributes to this goal. Moreover, commenters asserted that the rule creates different appeal deadlines for pretermitted cases, where cases pretermitted because of an applicable ACA are subject to the 10-day deadline and cases pretermitted due to, for example, failure to pay the fee or not adequately completing the application are subject to the longer 30-day deadline, which is inconsistent with the Department’s stated harmonization goal. Commenters further expressed that the IFR does not explain how disputes over the applicable deadline should be determined.

Response: The Department disagrees that appeal deadlines for cases involving asylum applications are confusing but nonetheless appreciates the opportunity to provide clarity. The INA requires that the Attorney General establish procedures for considering asylum applications “filed under” section 208(a) of the Act, 8 U.S.C. 1158(a). INA 208(d)(1), 8 U.S.C. 1158(d)(1). Those procedures must provide that “any administrative appeal shall be filed within 30 days of a decision granting or denying asylum, or within 30 days of the completion of removal proceedings before an immigration judge . . . whichever is later.” INA 208(d)(5)(A)(iv), 8 U.S.C. 1158 (d)(5)(A)(iv). But those procedures, including the 30-day appeal deadline, do not apply where an alien is ineligible to apply for asylum at all under section 208(a)(1) of the Act, 8 U.S.C. 1158(a)(1). Said differently, if an alien is ineligible to even apply for asylum pursuant to section 208(a)(1) of the Act, 8 U.S.C. 1158(a)(1), the alien is not entitled to subsequent procedures implementing a 30-day appeal deadline. See 91 FR 5272 n.15.

The INA provides three such scenarios in which an alien is barred from applying for asylum: (1) the alien may be removed to a safe third country pursuant to an agreement commonly referred to as an ACA; (2) the alien does not show by a preponderance of the evidence that his or her application has been filed within one year after the date of the alien’s arrival in the United States, subject to narrow exceptions; or (3) the alien has previously applied for asylum and had such application denied, subject to narrow exceptions. INA 208(a)(2)(A), (B), (C), 8 U.S.C. 1158(a)(2)(A), (B), (C).

Accordingly, in any case where an alien is deemed ineligible to apply for asylum pursuant to one of these three subparagraphs, the applicable appeal deadline, in accordance with this rule, is 10 days. This 10-day appeal period similarly applies to cases where application of these ineligibility provisions is followed by alternative substantive holdings denying asylum, as these ineligibility provisions serve as the baseline denial reason in addressing whether the alien is even eligible to apply for asylum. To use an example provided by commenters, if an Immigration Judge determines an alien is subject to the one-year bar and also concludes that the alien failed to establish a well-founded fear of future persecution, the 10-day deadline applies. In any other asylum case, the appeal deadline remains 30 days, consistent with the INA’s requirements. For clarity, in such cases, the 30-day appeal deadline attaches to the entire case, not to the asylum claim itself. Indeed, the relevant regulatory provision applies in “cases” where an Immigration Judge has adjudicated an asylum application and did not deny the application under 208(a)(2)(A), (B), or (C) of the Act, 8 U.S.C. 1158(a)(2)(A), (B), or (C)—not to individual claims within those cases. 91 FR 5278 (amending 8 CFR 1003.38(b)(2)). For example, in cases where an alien has applied for asylum, withholding of removal, and protection under the CAT regulations, if the alien’s asylum application was not denied due to application of an ACA, failure to apply for asylum within one year of entry, or because he or she previously has been denied asylum, the alien has 30 days to appeal the decision in his or her case, which includes all claims for relief and protection from removal.

Additionally, commenters’ assertion that the Department did not consider the “whichever is later” statutory language is incorrect. The Department analyzed the language in section 208(d)(5)(A)(iv) of the Act, 8 U.S.C. 1158(d)(5)(A)(iv), and determined that, for clarity 8 CFR 1003.38(b) should provide that the appeal filing period begins to run with the “date of the stating of an Immigration Judge’s oral decision or the mailing or electronic notification of an Immigration Judge’s written decision.” In rare cases, an Immigration Judge might adjudicate an asylum application earlier in the proceedings and then issue a final decision fully resolving removal proceedings at a later date. In these circumstances, the appeal period under 8 CFR 1003.38(b) would not begin to run until that later date because that is the date when the Immigration Judge completes the case, rather than simply disposing of a single claim. Thus, because the appeal period would begin to run from this later date, 8 CFR 1003.38(b) is consistent with the requirement in section 208(d)(5)(A)(iv) of the Act, 8 U.S.C. 1158(d)(5)(A)(iv), that the time period in which to appeal a decision granting or denying asylum run from “whichever [of the relevant dates] is later.” Accordingly, the Department believes that the language as drafted complies with the INA.

The Department further disagrees with commenters that it will be unclear which deadline applies to an asylum case because it will be unclear on what basis an Immigration Judge denies an asylum application. The Department is confident that Immigration Judges will clearly articulate any basis for denying an alien’s asylum application such that the applicable appeal-filing deadline will be readily apparent. Additionally, the Department expects that Immigration Judges will advise aliens of the applicable appeal deadline as part of the obligation to advise an alien of his or her appeal rights. See generally INA 240(c)(5), 8 U.S.C. 1229a(c)(5) (requiring the Immigration Judge, if ordering an alien removed, to “inform the alien of the right to appeal that decision”); 8 CFR 1240.10(a)(3) (requiring the Immigration Judge to “[a]scertain that the respondent has received a copy of appeal rights”); EOIR, Policy Manual, pt. II, ch. 3.15(h) (Feb. 10, 2026), https://www.justice.gov/eoir/policy-manual-eoir/part- II/icpm/chapter-3-15 [https://perma.cc/HK27-PJAZ] (stating that “the Immigration Judge informs the parties of the deadline for filing an appeal with the Board, unless the right to appeal is waived”).

Finally, commenters are correct that the changes to appeal filing deadlines will result in different appeal deadlines for asylum cases depending on the reason for denial. But the Department has determined that the different appeal deadlines for asylum cases— which are a function of statutory requirements and, thus, cannot be altered by EOIR—do not meaningfully detract from the Department’s appellate deadline harmonization goal. c. Additional Concerns with 10-day Appeal Deadline Comment: Commenters opposed decreasing the time to file an appeal with the Board to 10 days, describing the new deadline as unworkable, unrealistic, and not enough time to prepare and file a Notice of Appeal. Commenters expressed concern that the 10- day appeal deadline will exacerbate existing barriers to access to justice. Commenters also stated that the IFR did not provide any empirical evidence that the 30-day period in which to file an appeal has contributed to an increase in appeal filings or the Board’s backlog, pointing out that appeals tripled between 2015 and 2025 while the deadline to file an appeal was 30 days and asserting that such increase was likely related to immigration enforcement activity and evolving substantive law. Commenters said that, absent data showing the 30-day deadline drives delay, shortening the appeal deadline risks impairing access to appellate review without corresponding efficiency gains. Commenters also stated that the IFR puts pressure on Immigration Judges who are already overwhelmed by implicitly forcing them to produce immediate written decisions and a review-ready record to make appeals possible, which commenters alleged risks incentivizing rushed oral decisions and increasing post-hearing confusion, litigation, and motions.

Commenters also stated that the IFR does not explain whether Immigration Judges will inform aliens if the 10-day or 30-day deadline applies in their cases. Lastly, commenters believed that the use of electronic filing through the EOIR Courts & Appeals System (“ECAS”) was not sufficient to ameliorate their concerns. Response: The Department declines to retain the 30-day appeal deadline in all cases. The Department disagrees with commenters’ claims that the 10-day deadline is unworkable or unrealistic. First, as the Department explained in the IFR, other types of appeals before EOIR are already subject to a 10-day filing deadline. See 8 CFR 1003.6(c)(1) (10-day deadline for DHS to appeal an Immigration Judge’s order to maintain an automatic stay of a custody redetermination order pursuant to 8 CFR 1003.19(i)); 28 CFR 68.54(a) (10-day deadline to appeal Administrative Law Judge’s decision to Chief Administrative Hearing Officer). Second, the Board’s adoption of electronic filing in 2021, and the further expansion allowing pro se aliens to file Notices of Appeal with the Board, allow parties to submit a Notice of Appeal electronically, obviating the need to account for mail difficulties or delays in filing deadlines in the vast majority of Board cases. 91 FR 5272.

The Department does not find persuasive commenters’ arguments that the length of the appeal deadline is unrelated to the number of appeals filed or the backlog. Several factors contribute to how many appeals are filed in any given year. Although factors like the scope of immigration enforcement activity by DHS or changes in the substantive law as a result of Federal court decisions are outside the Department’s control, the Department can control its own procedures, like filing deadlines, to keep cases moving expeditiously before the Board. And the shortened appeal deadline—which applies equally to aliens and DHS—will work in concert with the expanded summary dismissal procedures to ensure that EOIR is efficiently and expeditiously completing appeals. See 91 FR 5272 (explaining that the 10-day deadline applies to both DHS and aliens “so neither side will be procedurally advantaged or disadvantaged by the change”). Further, as previously discussed, a 10-day deadline to file an administrative appeal of an Immigration Judge decision is not unprecedented: A 1987 rule set the regulatory deadline to file an appeal of a decision of an Immigration Judge at 10 days after service of the decision or 13 days if the decision was mailed. That rule was in place for almost a decade. See, e.g., 8 CFR 3.36(b) (1987); 52 FR 2935.

In 1996, EOIR established a centralized process for filing Notices of Appeal directly with the Board and increased the appeal deadline to 30 days. 61 FR 18903; 8 CFR 3.38(b) (1996). The Department increased the time frame to file an appeal to address concerns “regarding the sufficiency of time to initiate the appellate process” and concerns raised by Federal courts related to the 10-day filing period and the requirement that parties file a Notice of Appeal in one forum and pay the requisite fee in another forum. 61 FR 18903. But importantly, when implementing the 30-day deadline, the Department did not indicate that such a change was required by law. Rather, the deadline was implemented as a matter of policy, reflective of the Department’s judgment regarding the appropriate procedures at that time. The decision to now revert the deadline to 10 days is similarly reflective of the Department’s judgment that, as a matter of policy, the 10-day deadline, in combination with other streamlining measures implemented by this rule, is the best way for the Department to address present circumstances, which include a significant backlog of pending cases at the Immigration Courts and Board.

Regarding commenters’ concerns that some aliens may not understand the appeal deadline applicable to their cases, the Department does not believe that determining the applicable case deadline will be a challenge, as the appeal deadline will be 10 days in most cases, except for cases involving certain asylum applications.
