Nonetheless, the Department expects that Immigration Judges will advise aliens of the applicable appeal deadline as part of the obligation to advise an alien of his or her appeal rights. See INA 240(c)(5), 8 U.S.C. 1229a(c)(5) (requiring the Immigration Judge, if ordering an alien removed, to “inform the alien of the right to appeal that decision”); 8 CFR 1240.10(a)(3) (requiring the Immigration Judge to “[a]scertain that the respondent has received a copy of appeal rights”); see also EOIR, Policy Manual, pt. II, ch. 3.15(h) (Feb. 10, 2026), https://www.justice.gov/eoir/policy-manual-eoir/part-II/icpm/chapter-3-15 [https://perma.cc/HK27-PJAZ] (stating that “the Immigration Judge informs the parties of the deadline for filing an appeal with the Board, unless the right to appeal is waived”). Commenters’ concerns related to the 10-day deadline’s impact on Immigration Judges are misplaced, as this rule does not alter any requirements for an Immigration Judge when issuing a decision.

Next, the Department believes that the 10-day filing deadline is a key piece of efforts to streamline immigration proceedings and that a “deadline for filing a notice of appeal is essential for the overall working of an immigration court system in order to bring cases to a final conclusion.” Morales-Morales, 28 I&N Dec. at 716. Indeed, without deadlines, an alien could attempt to delay proceedings indefinitely. Id. “Moreover, ‘[f]iling deadlines, like statutes of limitations, necessarily operate harshly and arbitrarily with respect to individuals who fall just on the other side of them, but if the concept of a filing deadline is to have any content, the deadline must be enforced.’” Id. (quoting United States v. Locke, 471 U.S. 84, 101 (1985)).

Although this final rule does not change the general 10-day filing deadline, the Department notes that if the unique circumstances in a case warrant equitable tolling pursuant to the Board’s existing standards, nothing in this rule prevents the Board from accepting an untimely appeal through that mechanism. The Department believes that this existing authority is sufficient to address truly exceptional circumstances that may arise in an individual case and provides the Board with sufficient flexibility to account for the facts presented by each individual case.

Finally, to the extent that commenters expressed concerns about ECAS reliability, EOIR has provided clear guidance in the event of any technical issues affecting electronic filing. See 8 CFR 1003.3(g)(2) (addressing ECAS system outages for Board appeals). Comment: Commenters questioned the interplay between the 10-day appeal filing deadline and fee waiver requests. Specifically, commenters requested clarity on what happens in cases where a fee waiver is denied and whether the pre-existing 15-day cure period in 8 CFR 1003.8(a)(3) will still apply, as commenters stated it is unclear how the Board will construe this regulation in light of the 10-day deadline.

Response: Neither the IFR nor this final rule alters existing Board practice with respect to fee waivers. Aliens seeking a waiver of the appeal filing fee must file a fee waiver request, Form EOIR-26A, alongside the Notice of Appeal. 8 CFR 1003.8(a)(3). If the fee waiver request does not demonstrate an inability to pay, the appeal will not be considered properly filed, “provided the Board grants 15 days to re-file the rejected document with the filing fee or new fee waiver request and tolls any applicable filing deadline during the 15-day cure period.” Id. Accordingly, if an alien files a fee waiver request and Notice of Appeal prior to the 10-day deadline, if the fee waiver is denied, the alien will have 15 days to pay the filing fee or correct the filing.

Comment: Commenters stated that, in some cases, the Immigration Judge will signal an intention to rule a particular way from the bench but will expand on their reasoning through a written decision that is later mailed or uploaded. Commenters cited the precedential Board decision Matter of Iskandarani, 29 I&N Dec. 26 (BIA 2025), which, according to commenters, held that if the Immigration Judge issues an oral decision that is later memorialized in writing, the appeal deadline clock begins to run on the date of the oral decision. Commenters recommended that, because the alien’s Notice of Appeal—which will generally be their only communication with the Board—must be filed within 10 days, the filing deadline should not start to run with the issuance of the oral decision.

Response: Commenters misinterpreted the Board’s holding in Iskandarani, which merely held that when an Immigration Judge renders an oral decision, the appeal deadline begins on that date, regardless of any summary of the oral decision later provided to the alien. See 29 I&N Dec. at 28 (“An oral decision is not transformed into a written decision merely because the Immigration Judge prepares a memorandum summarizing the oral decision.”). When an Immigration Judge issues an oral decision, that is the official decision of the Immigration Judge for appeal purposes. Immigration Judges may also provide the parties with a summary of the oral decision’s holding, generally on an EOIR-provided template. But any accompanying summary is just that—a summary of the oral decision.

As such, this rule does not change EOIR’s existing regulations governing the issuance of Immigration Judge decisions or EOIR’s existing practice related to calculating when the time for an appeal begins to run. Immigration Judges may issue decisions orally or in writing. 8 CFR 1003.37(a). When issuing a decision orally, the Immigration Judge must state the decision in the presence of the parties, and “a memorandum summarizing the oral decision shall be served on the parties.” Id. In those cases, the time in which to file an appeal is calculated “from the date of the stating of an Immigration Judge’s oral decision.” 8 CFR 1003.38(b). As noted by commenters, the Board has held that the beginning of the appeal period in such cases “is unaffected by the subsequent mailing of a memorandum summarizing the oral decision.” Iskandarani, 29 I&N Dec. at 28.

The Department does not believe that the shortened appeal deadline presents concerns related to the issuance of oral decisions where aliens are represented. The alien and his or her representative will be present for the issuance of an oral decision, and representatives also have access to the hearing recording containing the oral decision through ECAS. The Department is confident that Immigration Judges will explain the bases for their decisions with clarity sufficient for aliens to identify any alleged errors of fact or law for Board appeals. Any subsequent written memorandum summarizing the oral decision is not intended to provide separate bases for appeal, although it may provide further explanation of points raised in the oral decision that may be used in any Notice of Appeal. See id. (noting that the memorandum summarizing the oral decision was not a separate written decision).

The Department has considered that, in some cases, the shortened appeal deadline may be less than optimal for certain unrepresented aliens to file a Notice of Appeal within 10 days when a decision is rendered orally. But in all cases, the alien will be present when an oral decision is issued, and the Department expects that Immigration Judges will deliver decisions to unrepresented aliens in a manner they understand, and aliens may use that knowledge when preparing and submitting a Notice of Appeal, consistent with longstanding practice. Aliens will also have additional time in which to review the decision if seeking further review in Federal court.

Congress entrusted decisions related to the conduct of removal proceedings to the Attorney General’s discretion. And given the unprecedented scope of the backlog of appeals pending before the Board, the shortened appeal deadline is necessary to ensure the efficient and expeditious processing of appeals; the benefit of implementing such changes outweighs any costs. See 91 FR 5276.

Comment: Commenters argued that two comparative 10-day appeal deadlines cited in the IFR—8 CFR 1003.6(c)(1) related to appeals of certain custody-related stays and 28 CFR 68.54(a) related to certain appeals before the Office of the Chief Administrative Hearing Officer—were not comparable to regular Board appeals because the former is only available to DHS and the latter is necessary under the relevant statutory framework.

Response: The Department cited those two EOIR provisions in the IFR to make the basic point that a 10-day appeal deadline is not unusual in EOIR administrative proceedings. See 91 FR 5272 (noting only that the 30-day Board appeal deadline “differs from other EOIR administrative appellate deadlines”). Separate from that point, the Department explained that a 10-day Board appeal deadline begins after an appellant’s claim has already been fully considered by EOIR at the Immigration Court and was broadly intended to improve the efficient consideration of Board appeals, particularly in light of the expansion of electronic filing with EOIR. See id.

3. Issue Waiver in Notice of Appeal Comment: Commenters raised concerns with the IFR’s appeal-waiver language in 8 CFR 1003.38(b)(3), which states that “[a]ny issue not raised in the Notice of Appeal from a Decision of an Immigration Judge (Form EOIR-26) shall be deemed waived.” Commenters argued that, particularly in combination with the 10-day filing deadline, this language risks forfeiture of meritorious issues on appeal, and that the risks would be greater for certain groups. Other commenters claimed that the appeal form now requires an entire page of legal arguments as to why the appeal is being filed, which, they asserted, transforms the Notice of Appeal into a legal brief.

Response: The Department disagrees with commenters’ concerns regarding the IFR’s waiver language in 8 CFR 1003.38(b)(3). Pre-existing regulations limit the Board to “resolv[ing] the questions before it.” See 8 CFR 1003.1(d)(1). To place an issue before the Board, aliens must provide the basis for their appeal for the Board to consider. See 8 CFR 1003.3(b) (“Statement of the basis of appeal.”). Similarly, pre-existing regulatory language already requires that a notice of appeal include sufficient specificity. Under current regulations, the notice must “specifically” identify the findings of fact, the conclusions of law, or both, that are being challenged, including, if applicable, “specific” contested facts and “specific” factual and legal findings. 8 CFR 1003.3(b). These requirements were not altered by the IFR and are well established. In short, the IFR does not change expectations or legal requirements regarding what information must be included in a Notice of Appeal and what the consequences are for omitting that information.

This rule’s waiver language in 8 CFR 1003.38(b) therefore merely states the obvious: a failure to raise an issue in the Notice of Appeal necessarily waives that issue. Although a shortened appellate period might require identifying those issues more quickly, stating the basis for an appeal is a baseline prerequisite without which the Board (or any appellate body) cannot function. Moreover, well-established Board precedent already treats issues not raised on appeal as waived, see, e.g., Matter of R-A-M-, 25 I&N Dec. 657, 658 n.2 (BIA 2012), the rule merely incorporates that precedent.

Commenters appeared to obliquely express concerns that the appeal-waiver language will indirectly cause aliens to fail to exhaust their administrative remedies for purposes of a subsequent petition for review pursuant to section 242(d)(1) of the Act, 8 U.S.C. 1252(d)(1). However, those concerns are not persuasive for several reasons. First, the Board already deems issues not raised on appeal to be waived, and aliens already encounter exhaustion hurdles pursuant to section 242(d)(1) of the Act, 8 U.S.C. 1252(d)(1). The rule does not alter that dynamic, nor does it prohibit aliens from arguing that they have exhausted their administrative remedies under the statute. Second, Federal circuit courts of appeal will ultimately set the binding interpretation of section 242(d)(1) of the Act, 8 U.S.C. 1252(d)(1), just as they do now. Because this provision of the rule merely codifies in regulation the status quo, the Department does not believe there is a basis for a circuit court to change its view of section 242(d)(1) of the Act, 8 U.S.C. 1252(d)(1); however, that is ultimately a question for those courts, and the Department cannot predict whether the new rule will cause them to revisit prior interpretations of that statute. The Department has merely considered the interaction between the rule and that statutory provision and found any concerns to be unavailing. Third, administrative exhaustion is inherently a fact-specific question. As such, the Department cannot state a general position on whether section 242(d)(1) of the Act, 8 U.S.C. 1252(d)(1), will bar review of an issue without reference to the specific facts of a particular case. Even general hypotheticals raised by commenters—e.g., pro se aliens—resist a generalized statement due to the nearly infinite number of factual permutations among a backlog of over 3 million cases.

Furthermore, contrary to commenters’ concerns, this rule does not address the Board’s longstanding specificity requirements with regard to issues raised on appeal. See 8 CFR 1003.1(d)(2)(i)(A) (stating that the Board may summarily dismiss any appeal or portion of any appeal in any case in which “the party concerned fails to specify the reasons for the appeal on Form EOIR-26 or Form EOIR-29 (Notices of Appeal) or other document filed therewith”); 8 CFR 1003.3(b) (reiterating same).

As explained by the Ninth Circuit, “[t]he purpose of the BIA’s strict specificity requirement is to ensure that the BIA is adequately apprised of the issues on appeal so that the BIA is not left to search through the record and speculate on what possible errors the [petitioner] claims.” Singh v. Gonzales, 416 F.3d 1006, 1010 (9th Cir. 2005) (cleaned up). Thus, “when the BIA receives ample specific advice about the reasons for an appeal, the BIA can deal promptly with appeals and focus resources on nonfrivolous appeals to reach a correct resolution.” See id.

This is a common sense understanding of the appellate process. For example, Federal courts follow the principle of party presentation, in that they “rely on the parties to frame the issues for decision and assign to courts the role of neutral arbiter of matters the parties present.” See United States v. Sineneng-Smith, 590 U.S. 371, 375 (2020). Similarly, the Board must be sufficiently apprised of the issues on appeal so that it can properly exercise its duties.

To be clear, this rule does not change the level of specificity required, it merely codifies the existing requirement that aliens must affirmatively raise issues on appeal to the Board or else risk waiver. In raising any relevant issues on appeal, existing specificity requirements apply. Just as before the IFR, aliens are not required to file a lengthy brief on each issue at the time the Notice of Appeal is filed. Rather, the appeal form must simply include enough specific information so that the Board can review the issues being appealed and, under this rule’s procedures, determine whether to accept the appeal en banc for full briefing and further review. See Form EOIR-26, Notice of Appeal from a Decision of an Immigration Judge, Sec. 6, (Sept. 2019), https://www.justice.gov/eoir/file/eoir26/dl [https://perma.cc/P3PP-7T3H] (“State in detail the reasons for this appeal.”); see also Nolasco-Amaya v. Garland, 14 F.4th 1007, 1012 (9th Cir. 2021) (alien must “provide meaningful guidance to the BIA by informing it of the issues contested on appeal; a generalized and conclusory statement about the proceedings before the [Immigration Judge] does not suffice”) (cleaned up). The pre-existing instructions for the Form EOIR-26 appeal form provide clear guidance on what such specificity entails: “Give specific details why you disagree with the Immigration Judge’s decision. Specify the findings of fact, the conclusions of law, or both, that you are challenging. If a question of law is presented, cite supporting legal authority. If the dispute is over the findings of fact, identify the specific facts you are challenging.” Form EOIR-26 Instructions, Section F (Sept. 2019), https://www.justice.gov/eoir/file/eoir26/dl [https://perma.cc/P3PP-7T3H].

4. Briefing Schedules Comments: Commenters raised concerns regarding the IFR’s briefing changes, including the simultaneous 20-day briefing schedule, the general prohibition on reply briefs, and the limitations on briefing extensions.

Commenters argued that, taken together, these changes would not leave aliens with sufficient time to fully present their arguments nor rebut arguments made by DHS counsel, though they did not explain why DHS would not be similarly disadvantaged. They also claimed that the Department did not consider the purposes underlying prior briefing schedules.

Commenters also noted that these briefing changes would force attorneys to compress complex briefing into truncated timelines, which would be further compounded if the attorneys were taking on representation for the first time on appeal to the Board. Commenters contended that limiting extensions to only “exceptional” circumstances of the alien—and not counsel—would reduce the amount of representation on appeal. Commenters also asserted that these changes would be particularly challenging for pro se and detained aliens, as well as UACs. Commenters suggested that the IFR not taking into account workload concerns for purposes of extending briefing schedules would impose difficulties on attorneys. Overall, commenters posited that the result of these briefing provisions would be to negatively impact the Board’s ability to produce well-reasoned decisions.

Commenters argued that sequential briefing and reply briefs would benefit the Board under the summary dismissal provisions of this rule, since the rule focuses Board resources on cases with novel or complex legal issues. Commenters suggested that if the Department was to move forward with simultaneous briefing in all cases, reply briefs would serve a more important purpose than they did previously. Commenters also stated that the Department did not acknowledge that reply briefs serve an important role before other appellate bodies, including Federal courts. Commenters claimed the tradeoff in quality for expediency is not worthwhile and would lead to erroneous decision-making in cases the Board does decide to adjudicate.

Finally, commenters noted possible alternatives to these briefing changes, including increasing EOIR staffing levels and expanding the use of motions to reopen or reconsider before an Immigration Judge.
Response: The Department has considered commenters’ concerns regarding the IFR’s briefing schedule changes but does not believe that any stated concerns outweigh the rule’s benefits.

First, the Board has long used simultaneous briefing for detained cases without incident. See Board of Immigration Appeals: Procedural Reforms to Improve Case Management, 67 FR 54878, 54904 (Aug. 26, 2002) (implementation of simultaneous briefing for detained aliens). Moreover, since the simultaneous briefing requirement of the IFR went into effect in March 2026, there has been no notable change in the quality of briefs or the handling of cases. Of course, in reviewing the comments on this rule, the Department understands that an attorney would wish to request as much time as possible to file and respond to briefs. But, as the Amica court noted in litigation over the IFR, “Plaintiffs offer no evidence . . . that [the pre-IFR simultaneous briefing requirement in detained cases has] proven unworkable.” 822 F. Supp. 3d at 167. Similarly, since March 2026, there is scant evidence that simultaneous briefing has proven unworkable. The Department agrees with the Amica court: the Board has longstanding expertise in adjudicating administrative appeals and has found simultaneous briefing sufficient to address the relevant issues on appeal. As explained in the IFR, simultaneous briefing “provides both parties sufficient opportunity to address any issues needed to be resolved on appeal or to identify any reasons for opposing the appeal, while balancing the need to expeditiously resolve the case.” 91 FR 5273.

As to reply briefs, the Board retains the discretion to accept further briefing as needed. See 8 CFR 1003.3(c). Thus, under this rule, once the Board has accepted a case for full briefing and further review, the Board can review the evidence and briefs provided and determine whether the facts of the particular case warrant additional briefing. Allowing reply briefs as standard practice merely delays adjudication in the many cases where the Board does not require further argument. Moreover, as with simultaneous briefing, the general prohibition on reply briefs has not proven unworkable or problematic since it went into effect in March 2026.

Third, limitations on briefing extensions are necessary to ensure that the Board efficiently perfects the record so that Board members can begin adjudicating appeals within the prescribed timelines. See generally 8 CFR 1003.1(e)(8) (Board adjudication timeline requirements). Notwithstanding EOIR’s longstanding policy that briefing extensions are disfavored, under the prior “good cause” standard, see, e.g., 8 CFR 1003.3(c)(1) (2002) (“The Board, upon written motion, may extend the period for filing a brief or a reply brief for up to 90 days for good cause shown.”), attorneys often came to feel entitled to a briefing extension as a matter of course, even when the basis was entirely foreseeable and raised only at the last minute. In the IFR, the Department tightened the standard to ensure that briefing extensions are provided only when truly necessary. The Department also believes that prohibiting “workload concerns” as a reason for an extension is consistent with both common sense and an attorney’s responsibility not to take on more work than the attorney can reasonably handle. See, e.g., 8 CFR 1003.102(q)(1) (stating that a “practitioner’s workload must be controlled and managed so that each matter can be handled competently”); see also ABA Model Rules of Professional Responsibility, Rule 1.3, comment 2 (“A lawyer’s work load must be controlled so that each matter can be handled competently.”). Indeed, in the Board’s experience, many attorneys routinely seek briefing extensions citing workload concerns, suggesting an alarming pattern of problematic behavior. A de facto entitlement to a briefing extension could inadvertently encourage practitioners to take on more cases than they can handle and violate their professional responsibility obligations.

The Department also clarifies a potential point of confusion: under this rule, the briefing schedule only begins once the Board has determined not to summarily dismiss an appeal and instead has accepted it for full briefing and further review. For example, in a case where the Board accepts an appeal for such briefing and review and transcripts are ordered, attorneys will often have a significant amount of time to prepare a brief. As such, the Department does not share commenters’ concerns that a stricter standard for briefing extensions will result in fewer represented aliens or lower-quality briefing. Further, the Department has not been presented with evidence that such concerns have materialized since March 2026 when that portion of the IFR went into effect. Taken together, the IFR’s briefing provisions fully allow the Board to make well- informed and well-reasoned decisions. And, despite commenters’ claims to the contrary, in no way do these procedures rise to the level of a due process violation. See, e.g., Gutierrez v. Holder, 662 F.3d 1083, 1091 (9th Cir. 2011) (explaining that, to violate due process, procedures must be “so fundamentally unfair that the alien was prevented from reasonably presenting his case”); Singh v. Ashcroft, 362 F.3d 1164, 1168 (9th Cir. 2004) (finding due process violation where alien was prevented from filing a brief after Board mailed briefing schedule to wrong address).

Under these changes, aliens fully retain their ability to file a brief in cases accepted for full briefing and further consideration by the Board, thus satisfying their opportunity to raise alleged issues with the Immigration Judge’s decision. Moreover, due process does not require reply briefs. Initial briefs are intended to raise any alleged issues at the Immigration Judge level and provide the parties with the opportunity to be heard; the Board can choose to request further briefing if additional clarification is needed. And simultaneous briefing in detained cases has been in effect at the Board for decades without issue—and no court, to the Department’s knowledge, has deemed simultaneous briefing in such cases a due process violation.

Separately, the Department does not believe commenters’ proposed alternatives would be viable substitutes for the rule’s briefing-schedule changes. Although EOIR is increasing its staffing, including administrative support staff at the Board, ultimately, hiring is controlled by the Congressional budget process and is well beyond the scope of this rule. Additionally, the increased usage of motions practice before the Immigration Courts would not impact the efficiency of the Board, which is the subject of this rule. Lastly, in response to commenters’ claims that the “exceptional circumstances” briefing extension language only applies to aliens and not their counsel, the Department reiterates for clarity this rule’s language that workload concerns, travel plans, or similar concerns within the control of either party “or their representatives” do not constitute exceptional circumstances. 8 CFR 1003.3(c)(1). This language is clear that exceptional circumstances may therefore apply to counsel but must still meet the requisite exceptionality as described in section 240(e)(1) of the Act, 8 U.S.C. 1229a(e)(1).

5. Transcription Procedures Comment: Some commenters raised concerns about the IFR’s elimination of Immigration Judge transcript review in 8 CFR 1003.5. Commenters asserted that removing the ability of Immigration Judges to review hearing transcripts for Board appeals will leave errors uncorrected on the record and heighten the risk of mistakes in the record. Commenters also contended that this change would place a burden on aliens to request copies of the Digital Audio Recordings (“DAR”) of their proceedings. As a result, commenters argued, this would lead to erroneous Board decisions and, in turn, incorrect removal orders.

Response: The Department disagrees regarding the effects of eliminating Immigration Judge transcript review. Immigration Judge transcript review in EOIR’s regulations is a vestige of outdated technology at the Immigration Courts from a time when hearings were manually recorded on tapes. See 67 FR 54878–901 (2002 rulemaking adding Immigration Judge transcript review timelines). Now, EOIR’s courtrooms use advanced digital recording technology, which produces significantly better recordings and lessens the potential for mistakes in subsequent transcription.30 And, to the extent there are potential mistakes in any transcriptions, there are longstanding procedures for addressing such mistakes, rather than having busy Immigration Judges take time away from their dockets to pore over transcripts for typographical errors. See EOIR Policy Manual, pt. III, ch. 3.2(f)(3) (Mar. 18, 2026), https://www.justice.gov/eoir/policy-manual-eoir/part-III/bia/chapter-3-2 [https://perma.cc/HWM3-9QDP]. Obvious defects should be brought to the attention of the Board’s Clerk’s Office. Id. Where the Clerk’s Office does not or cannot remedy the defects and the party believes the defect to be significant to the party’s argument or the adjudication of the appeal, the party should identify the defect and argue its significance with specificity in the appeal brief for the Board to consider. Id. Further, there is no practical purpose to Immigration Judge transcription review. Immigration Judges cannot make substantive changes to transcripts without potentially violating due process, and requiring Immigration Judges to review transcripts solely to correct typographical errors is a waste of adjudicatory resources.

Additionally, commenters’ argument regarding the necessity of requesting a copy of the DAR is unrelated to the transcription-review change described above. As it relates to transcription, this rule makes only a small modification to remove Immigration Judge transcription review during the transcript production process at the Board. Once produced, that transcript is made available to the parties and any transcription errors can then be addressed by the parties. None of this happens at the initial Notice of Appeal stage, so commenters’ arguments regarding the availability of a copy of the DAR at that point are irrelevant to this rule.

30 Press Release, EOIR Completes Digital Audio Recording Implementation (Sept. 2, 2010), https://www.justice.gov/sites/ default/files/pages/attachments/2015/ 08/20/eoircompletesdar09022010.pdf [https://perma.cc/EMK4-QSY9] (“This new system improves the quality of recordings and transcriptions through the use of more microphones throughout each courtroom.”).

Finally, the Department is making a minor, technical edit to 8 CFR 1003.1(e)(3) to avoid confusion regarding the production of transcripts. That section currently states that “[i]n any case that has not been summarily dismissed, the case management system shall arrange for the prompt completion of the record of proceeding and transcript, and the issuance of a briefing schedule, as appropriate.” There may be confusion surrounding the concluding phrase “as appropriate” and whether it modifies “transcript,” leaving the incorrect impression that the provision requires the production of a transcript in all cases. However, the Board has for many years considered several types of appeals that do not have transcripts. Thus, the Department is making a minor edit to 8 CFR 1003.1(e)(3) to make it clear that the Board will produce a transcript only in cases not subject to summary dismissal and where a transcript is otherwise warranted, which excludes those where the Board has historically not created a transcript.

6. Other Procedural Changes Comment: A few commenters disagreed with the IFR’s changes to remove the Chief Appellate Immigration Judge’s ability to extend adjudication deadlines or hold certain cases. Commenters stated that this change eliminates flexibility, particularly in managing complex or time-sensitive appeals. Commenters also argued that removing the ability to hold a case pending resolution of a Federal court case, including a Supreme Court case, would create inefficiencies, stating that aliens would effectively have to file a motion to reopen or an additional appeal after the new controlling decision is issued. Separately, another commenter raised concerns with the IFR’s harmonization of the 90- and 180-day Board adjudication timelines to both start from when the record is complete. The commenter stated that these timelines will prolong the backlog because this rule only applies prospectively to new cases. The commenter also claimed that further assignment of cases not meeting the deadlines to the Chief Appellate Immigration Judge or Deputy Chief Appellate Immigration Judge will only lead to rushed decisionmaking.

Response: This rule was promulgated to address significant backlogs facing the Board, with a particular aim of reducing any delays in adjudicating cases before the Board. One means to that end is reducing rarely used mechanisms that provide for delays in certain circumstances. Fundamentally, in light of the significant backlog facing the Board, appeals must be adjudicated within the timelines provided, see 8 CFR 1003.1(e)(8), or else the Board will never be able to gain control of its caseload. Moreover, in removing the hold provision, the Department recognizes a simple maxim— cases ready to be adjudicated should be adjudicated—and not delayed pending some uncertain outside action beyond the agency’s control. Otherwise, as the Department learned from the past use of administrative closure, for example, delays can quickly compound into crises. See EOIR, PM 25-29, Cancellation of Director’s Memorandum 22-03 (Apr. 18, 2025), https://www.justice.gov/eoir/media/1397161/dl?inline [https://perma.cc/SH9J-CKXL] (“Administrative closure merely ‘kicks the can down the road,’ increasing the overall backlog while leaving ripple effects—e.g. multiple continuances and lost adjudication time—in its wake, which further exacerbate the backlog.”).

With regard to the harmonization of the adjudication timelines, the commenter misread the effect of this rule. The adjudication timelines and further referral processes already existed in EOIR’s regulations. For consistency, this rule merely modifies the date on which the record is deemed complete for these adjudication timelines to begin running.

Finally, as with other changes made by the IFR that were allowed to go into effect in March 2026, these changes have not created any notable issues or concerns with Board procedures or case processing.

7. Terminology Comment: Commenters disagreed with the IFR’s replacement of “noncitizen” and “unaccompanied child” with “alien” and “unaccompanied alien child,” respectively. Commenters claimed the use of the term “alien” is pejorative and is a rhetorical move towards more dehumanizing language as compared to neutral, immigration-status focused words like “noncitizen.” Response: The terms “noncitizen” and “unaccompanied child” are inconsistent with the statutory language. “Alien” is the statutory term defined in the INA and uniformly used throughout title 8 of the United States Code. See generally INA, 8 U.S.C. 1101 et seq. (using the term “alien,” not “noncitizen,” when referring to persons who are not citizens or nationals of the United States). Similarly, the term “unaccompanied alien child” has a specific statutory definition, see 6 U.S.C. 279(g)(2), that is not fully captured by the term “unaccompanied child.” Retaining the terms “noncitizen” and “unaccompanied child” would be inconsistent even within EOIR’s regulations, as, without amendment, chapter V of title 8 of the CFR would sometimes refer to aliens as “noncitizens” and other times as “aliens.” See generally 8 CFR Ch. V. The terms “noncitizen” and “unaccompanied child” are also inconsistent with DHS regulations, which continue to use the term “alien.” See generally 8 CFR Ch. I. Further exacerbating the risk of confusion, the term “noncitizen” is not a precise synonym for the term “alien.” See EOIR PM 25-07, Cancellation of Policy Memorandum 21-27, 4 & n.4 (Jan. 29, 2025), https://www.justice.gov/eoir/media/1387446/dl?inline [https://perma.cc/HU2H- V2TF]. The INA defines the term “alien” to mean a person who is neither a citizen nor a national of the United States. INA 101(a)(3), 8 U.S.C. 1101(a)(3). The term “noncitizen” does not recognize the full scope of people who are “aliens” because the term “noncitizen” includes “national[s] of the United States,” who are individuals “who, though not [ ] citizen[s] of the United States, owe[] permanent allegiance to the United States.” INA 101(a)(22), 8 U.S.C. 1101(a)(22). Thus, a plain-language understanding of the term “noncitizen” is incongruous with its usage in the CFR prior to this amendment. Indeed, caselaw shows that these imprecise terms do not in fact have a well- settled meaning, and their use risks creating confusion through imprecision, in addition to improperly suggesting that longstanding and well-defined statutory terms are imbued with pejorative meaning. See Khan v. Garland, 69 F.4th 265, 272 (5th Cir. 2023) (Ho, J., concurring) (“[I]n the context of immigration law, we use ‘alien,’ not to disparage one’s character—or to denote one’s planetary origin—but to describe one’s legal status.”). By contrast, the term “alien” has a long-established usage and settled understanding. Id. (describing the term “alien” as “a centuries-old legal term found in countless judicial decisions” dating back to the 1800s). The legal status of alienage is fundamental to EOIR’s authority to exercise jurisdiction over an individual and is at the core of all proceedings, including findings of removability and orders of removal, as well as forms of eligibility for relief and protection from removal.

As Judge Bea, himself a naturalized citizen, stated in his concurrence in Avilez v. Garland: “These distinctions matter. Words matter. Our federal immigration statutes concern themselves with aliens. This word is not a pejorative nor an insult.” 69 F.4th 525, 544 (9th Cir. 2023). Judge Bea went on to state that “when used in its statutory context,” the world “alien” “admits of its statutory definition, not those definitions with negative connotations that can be plucked at will from the dictionary.” Id. Regulations should reflect the statutes they implement and apply, so using the same terms avoids any confusion over the relevant populations being addressed by regulation. Any suggestions that such changes are the result of animus are unfounded. Any concerns about that language are more appropriately directed to Congress. D. Effects of Rule

1. Impacts to Federal Courts Comment: Commenters asserted that the IFR’s changes will, in effect, shift a large portion of the Board’s work and the backlog of pending appeals to the Federal courts as the only remaining mechanism available to aliens to substantively challenge an Immigration Judge’s decision. Commenters stated that this shift will result in increased habeas petitions and remands back to the Board, thus inundating the Federal court system with more PFRs and increasing the likelihood of judicial error. Commenters argued that this shift violates due process, the INA, and the Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act (“TVPRA”). Commenters also posited that this rule would shield agencies from the Equal Access to Justice Act (“EAJA”) by accelerating removals and creating defective records that would inhibit successful challenges to unlawful detention and prevent the recovery of attorneys’ fees.
Commenters anticipated, without citing any evidence, that aliens whose appeals are summarily dismissed will file PFRs at a higher rate than those whose appeals are dismissed on the merits.

Commenters argued that an increased immigration caseload before the Federal courts would ultimately result in the less efficient resolution of cases because the Federal courts would be overwhelmed by the volume of the cases coming before them, which could total in the millions of cases. Specifically, commenters explained that without transcripts, Federal courts may lack the factual record necessary to evaluate credibility findings, evidentiary rulings, or the basis for the Immigration Judge’s decision, thus generating delays and procedural complications.

Commenters also asserted an increase in PFRs with Federal courts would require the Department to assign more attorneys, or attorneys outside of the Office of Immigration Litigation, to handle the surge in PFRs. Concomitantly, commenters alleged that this surge in PFRs would be accompanied by a significant reduction in the number of attorneys available to represent aliens on appeal because appearances before Federal courts are subject to specific requirements that are not applicable to practice before EOIR.

Response: As an initial matter, the Department notes that Congress created a statutory scheme for Federal court review of removal orders, see INA 242, 8 U.S.C. 1252, and to the extent that commenters have concerns about the impacts to Federal courts within that statutory scheme, including the amount of time to consider such appeals, docketing practices before the Federal courts, development of the record before the Federal courts, or decisions issued by the Federal courts, such concerns are both wholly speculative and outside of the scope of this rulemaking.

Commenters’ views about a potential surge in Federal court PFRs are illogical and unfounded. Although the initial rate at which PFRs are filed may temporarily increase due to this rule, that rate would stabilize over time as courts and practitioners became accustomed to the new procedures. More importantly, the overall number of PFRs over time would not be expected to change, and commenters did not advance a persuasive argument as to why it should. As the IFR explained, even if all appeals were adjudicated with full briefing, there would be two general outcomes: (1) some cases would be decided in the alien’s favor, in which case no PFR would be filed because Board decisions in the alien’s favor cannot be reviewed by Federal courts; and (2) some cases would be decided adversely to the alien, in which case an alien might file a PFR. See 91 FR 5272 n.14. The summary dismissal provisions of this rule do not change those two expected outcomes. In cases where the Board summarily dismisses an appeal where the Immigration Judge’s decision was erroneously adverse to the alien, the Board’s decision not to further consider the appeal would mean that the alien might file a PFR to contest the adverse agency action, just as they could have prior to the IFR after an adverse Board decision. Meanwhile, in cases where the Board summarily dismisses an Immigration Judge’s decision that was erroneously favorable to the alien and adverse to DHS, the failure of the Board to correct the decision would mean no PFR would be filed, because, as just noted, there is no Federal court review of cases erroneously decided in the alien’s favor. Thus, although it is possible that this rule might change the timing of PFRs, the Department anticipates that there would be minimal to no impact on the volume of PFRs over time.

Moreover, even if there were an increase in PFRs, it would be more appropriately viewed as a byproduct of this rule’s increasing efficiencies and should not be considered a negative result. Specifically, because the Department expects EOIR to render final administrative adjudications more swiftly due to this rule’s provisions, aliens will much more efficiently be able to raise any available challenges to the agency determination for resolution before the Federal courts. Specific concerns related to the Department’s staffing, including in the Office of Immigration Litigation, are outside the scope of this rulemaking, but the Department notes it has considered the impact of this rule’s changes on Department resources necessary to handle immigration matters in Federal court. Likewise, the Department has similarly considered any impacts to the availability of private counsel and finds any concerns regarding potential unavailability at the PFR stage wholly speculative. Additionally, any resource constraints faced by the Federal courts in adjudicating cases within their Congressionally mandated jurisdiction, see INA 242, 8 U.S.C. 1252, are both outside the scope of this rulemaking and outside the control of the Department.

With respect to commenters’ concerns about potential impacts to EOIR, such as predictions of dramatic increases in remands to the agency, these concerns are both speculative and unsupported by current operations. As stated in the IFR, on substantive review the Board generally agrees with Immigration Judge decisions in the overwhelming majority of cases—a conclusion that is unchallenged by commenters. Thus, even before this rule, Federal courts were already often considering the Immigration Judge’s reasoning when considering PFRs. Accordingly, the Department does not expect there to be a dramatic shift in the number of cases remanded to the agency where the Board summarily dismisses an appeal, similarly leaving the Immigration Judge’s decision undisturbed. And even if there were to be a modest increase in the number of remands to the Board, the IFR’s fundamental changes to make the appellate process more efficient outweigh the negatives of any such increase. Comment: Commenters also expressed concern with the sufficiency of the record to be reviewed by the Federal courts. Specifically, commenters stated that the Federal courts would largely conduct the first substantive appellate review of cases without the benefit of prior briefing by the parties or legal analysis by the Board, which would deprive the Federal courts of the agency’s analysis that, in commenters’ view, is needed to undertake meaningful judicial review.

According to commenters, because the Board creates transcripts only in cases that are not summarily dismissed, the administrative record received by the Federal courts will not contain a transcript of the underlying proceedings or the Immigration Judge’s oral decision, thereby preventing the appellate court from reviewing testimony or the basis for the order of removal. Lastly, commenters argued that the rulemaking should explain how transcripts and oral decisions will be provided after an alien files a PFR. Response: The Department will comply with all statutory requirements for submitting the appellate record for cases being considered by the Federal courts. See, e.g., INA 242(b)(2), 8 U.S.C. 1252(b)(2); Fed. R. App. P. 17(b). It will also provide transcripts in all cases where it otherwise would have provided a transcript if the Board had decided the case under prior procedures. The specific transcription process, including contract services and the provision of transcripts internally to submit the administrative record, are beyond the scope of this rulemaking, and the Department declines to specify them.

Further, the Department notes that the statute also sets forth requirements for parties before the Federal courts, such as the required submission of briefs. See INA 242(b)(3)(C), 8 U.S.C. 1252(b)(3)(C); see also Fed. R. App. P. 28, 31 (setting briefing requirements). Thus, irrespective of whether briefs have been submitted to the Board, the Federal courts will have the benefit of briefing for all issues subject to Federal court review. Moreover, any relevant agency record will be available for purposes of review before the Federal courts and, to the extent that aliens have concerns over the adequacy of the record, such arguments can be directed to the Federal courts, which can hold the case for the filing of the complete record or remand where the record is incorrect or incomplete.

Comment: Commenters posited that aliens could bypass the Board altogether and file a PFR directly with a Federal court, as the INA requires aliens to exhaust only administrative remedies that are available as of right, and not contingent on permission or discretion. See Santos-Zacaria, 598 U.S. at 424. Thus, according to commenters, the Federal courts would become the default venue for review, flooding the Federal courts with PFRs and stays of removal, and resulting in extensive backlogs.

Response: Any concerns regarding interpretations of the INA’s exhaustion requirements are properly raised before the Federal courts, to whom such requirements apply. See INA 242(d)(1), 8 U.S.C. 1252(d)(1). As the Department explained in the IFR, when an appeal is summarily dismissed under the provisions added by this rule, the Department intends that the Immigration Judge’s decision become the final agency decision for purposes of Federal court review, unless the Attorney General exercises discretion to review under 8 CFR 1003.1(h). In any PFR of a final removal order under section 242(a)(1) of the Act, 8 U.S.C. 1252(a)(1), following a summary dismissal by the Board, the Department expects that the Federal courts would review the substance of the Immigration Judge’s decision as the basis for the final order. Thus, this rule does not change any existing understanding regarding when a removal order becomes final or when a PFR must be filed.

Comment: Some commenters suggested possible alternatives, arguing, for example, that if the Federal courts are the appropriate venue to adjudicate appeals, then the entirety of immigration proceedings should be removed from the control of the Department. Commenters also suggested that if the Department eliminated the Board’s jurisdiction over appeals of motions to reopen and reconsider, aliens would be able to file a PFR of such decisions directly with the Federal courts, which would result in only a comparatively minimal increase in PFRs.

Response: Commenters’ recommendations are beyond the scope of this rulemaking and the Department’s authority. Congress has provided for a system of administrative hearings for immigration cases, and the Department cannot change that system. See generally INA 240, 8 U.S.C. 1229a (establishing administrative procedures for removal proceedings); cf. Strengthening and Reforming America’s Immigration Court System: Hearing before the Subcomm. on Border Sec. & Immigration of the S. Comm. on the Judiciary, 115th Cong. 1 (2018) (written response to Questions for the Record of James McHenry, Director, Executive Office for Immigration Review) (“The financial costs and logistical hurdles to implementing an Article I immigration court system would be monumental and would likely delay pending cases even further.”). Because commenters’ claims are unfounded in law or practice and well beyond the scope of this rulemaking, the Department declines to make any revisions to the rule on the basis of such claims.

Commenters’ recommendations to remove Board jurisdiction over appeals of Immigration Judge denials of motions to reopen or reconsider are outside of the scope of this rulemaking, which addresses the procedures for filing and consideration of appeals before the Board and does not address the Board’s jurisdiction.

2. Harm to Specific Populations Comments: Commenters asserted that the Department did not consider the IFR’s impact on specific vulnerable populations, including pro se aliens; detained aliens; indigent aliens; alien children, including UACs, those eligible for Special Immigrant Juvenile visas (“SIJ”), and U.S. citizen children with at least one parent without legal immigration status; aliens with mental illnesses or disabilities; aliens at risk of gender- based violence or human trafficking; non-English speaking or low-literacy aliens; communities of color; asylum-seekers; and pro bono organizations or providers. In general, commenters argued that the IFR would disproportionately harm these populations by denying them access to legal counsel, meaningful review of their proceedings, and a reasonable opportunity to fully assert their claims on appeal. First, commenters stated that the Department did not consider the impact of the IFR’s shorter deadlines, lack of guaranteed merits review, and limited briefing opportunities on pro se aliens. Commenters additionally highlighted the difficulty of accessing the Federal courts for a pro se alien, who, according to commenters, would be unable to navigate the complex and stringent procedural requirements of filing a PFR. Commenters claimed that due to the lack of automatic stays of removal in Federal court, pro se aliens will struggle to successfully seek a stay of removal on appeal. Commenters also contested the IFR’s assumption that pro se aliens have access to its electronic filing system to file a Notice of Appeal, stating that only attorneys and Accredited Representatives can access ECAS and that EOIR is still phasing enrollment for the analogous Respondent Access Portal, so pro se aliens are only eligible to register if they receive an official notice of eligibility by mail. Relatedly, commenters noted that the Form EOIR-26, Notice of Appeal, is not available through the Respondent Access Portal. Commenters also asserted that, even for those aliens who have enrolled in the Respondent Access Portal before the Immigration Judge issues the decision, the Respondent Access Portal does not grant unrepresented aliens access to the DAR of the proceedings.

Second, commenters stated that detained aliens will be adversely and disproportionately impacted by the IFR and the shortened appeal timeline. Specifically, commenters argued that detained appellants may be unable to, or severely limited in, timely appealing an Immigration Judge decision due to restrictions in accessing counsel, phones, mail, legal libraries, and writing materials, all of which could stifle the filing of timely and legally sufficient Notices of Appeal. Commenters claimed that detained respondents are subject to pervasive technological and communications issues, including expensive and unreliable telephone calls to discuss legal matters, lack of access to email and electronic messaging, barriers to in-person visits, and delays in mail related to their legal proceedings, thus interfering with their timely receipt of notice of an Immigration Judge’s decision and their ability to file their Notice of Appeal or conduct legal research to file briefs.

Third, commenters stated that indigent aliens with limited financial resources will be unable to procure the financial support necessary to afford filing fees and representation within the shortened appeal period proposed by the IFR, particularly in light of the recently increased cost of filing appeals, and may lack computers for electronic record review or filing. Commenters asserted that the combination of high filing fees, shortened deadlines, and representation costs creates layered financial barriers that undermine meaningful access to appellate review for any aliens, but especially indigent aliens.
Fourth, commenters argued that the IFR will negatively impact children.

Specifically, commenters stated that the IFR will significantly reduce UACs’ and alien children’s ability to secure counsel in time or to sufficiently represent themselves before the Board. Commenters added that the IFR creates a confusing two-tiered system for appeal windows that is compounded by the statutory protections in place for UACs and alien child asylum seekers and ignores the heightened risk of errors in cases with UACs and alien children. Commenters generally stated that UACs and alien children lack the developmental capacity, legal knowledge, financial resources, and practical ability to navigate the changes delineated in the IFR.

Commenters further claimed that the IFR will adversely impact U.S. citizen children with at least one parent without immigration status and children eligible for SIJ visas. Commenters asserted that, due to the increased removals of aliens as a result of the IFR, U.S. citizen children with at least one parent will suffer mental health and long-term developmental impacts “as they fear one or both parents could be arrested, detained, or deported.” Further, such U.S. citizen children, according to commenters, also risk being suddenly placed in State child welfare systems if their caregivers are detained, further exacerbating these issues. Additionally, commenters claimed that increased instances of family separation due to the IFR will prevent children eligible for SIJ visas from “seeking protection from abuse, abandonment, or neglect” if the caregiver whose care they are living under is ordered removed.

Fifth, commenters asserted that aliens with mental illnesses or disabilities and aliens dealing with trauma-related difficulties will struggle to meet tighter appeal deadlines and identify issues on appeal due to their diminished capacity and lack of legal sophistication.

Sixth, commenters contended that this rule would disproportionately impact low- literacy and non-English-speaking aliens. Commenters posited that, in addition to completing the requirements for appeal, aliens who do not speak or read in English must also obtain translations or interpretation of the Immigration Judge’s decision to understand the status of their case and the options available to them, which would be impossible to do within the IFR’s appeal timeframe. Commenters noted that aliens must also translate their claims to complete the Form EOIR-26, Notice of Appeal, which is only offered in English and must be filled out in English. Commenters claimed that aliens who speak rare languages face additional barriers and will not have time to access interpretation or translation of documents under the IFR.

Seventh, commenters generally asserted that the IFR would negatively impact communities of color, leading to greater racial and economic disparities and undermining access to justice. One commenter claimed that the IFR would disproportionately impact Southeast Asians, who are uniquely situated within the immigration enforcement system due to the intersection of forced displacements, resettlement conditions, and criminalization. That commenter argued that the IFR will accelerate deportations of Southeast Asians by reducing critical safeguards against legal error.

Eighth, commenters argued that the IFR will negatively impact asylum seekers due to limitations on appeals resulting in the removal of individuals eligible for asylum without meaningful appellate oversight. Some commenters claimed that asylum seekers would lack time to gather evidence and build their cases on appeal. Commenters worried that the two distinct deadlines for asylum appeals will cause confusion for asylum seekers already navigating a complex system. Specifically, commenters emphasized that the IFR is silent as to whether aliens will be provided with notice of which deadline applies to their asylum appeal. Some commenters noted that asylum-seeking alien children will lack an opportunity for meaningful review of their cases and the opportunity to challenge legal error when their applications are denied based on ACA grounds, the one-year filing bar, or other application bars because ten days is an insufficient amount of time for a child to prepare a claim or find an attorney.

Lastly, commenters stated that organizations that serve pro se and indigent aliens are already strained, and that this rule will diminish their capacity to effectively and ethically represent clients by creating a conflict between procedural compliance and ethical duties. Commenters further argued that practice before the Federal courts is extremely different from practice before EOIR and few organizations have sufficient staff admitted to the bars of Federal courts of appeals to handle PFRs.

With regard to possible alternatives to reduce the impact on the populations noted above, some commenters suggested incorporating safeguards into the IFR, including automatic extensions for detained aliens and acceptance of a “short form protective” Notice of Appeal followed by a supplemental statement of issues, in recognition of the significant logistical barriers to communicating with counsel, reviewing records, and securing required signatures.

Response: The Department has considered the impact of the rule on all of the populations raised by commenters and has thoroughly reviewed the concerns raised. In general, the commenters’ concerns relate to the hypothetical experiences of individuals in unusual, isolated circumstances, or policy disagreements that already exist under the current regulations. The commenters’ concerns about these hypothetical scenarios and differing policy views are not persuasive. Furthermore, the Department has concluded that even if the concerns raised are factually accurate and accurately reflect the law and practice, those concerns—both singularly and cumulatively—are nonetheless outweighed by the salutary efficiency benefits of the rule.

The agency recognizes that no rule can cover every single possible scenario regarding an alien population currently in immigration proceedings of approximately 3.5 million, each of whom is differently situated in terms of background, education level, immigration status, English proficiency, personal characteristics, sophistication, representation status or desire for representation, and availability of relief. Many of these permutations have been raised by commenters, and there will inevitably be others, too. However, the potential existence of unique cases, which can be addressed through other means on a case-by-case basis, is insufficient to outweigh the efficiency benefits generated by this rule. In short, the agency has considered all of the commenters’ concerns and acknowledges that there may be individual cases in which commenters’ concerns are validated; however, as a policy matter, those concerns are outweighed by the benefits of the rule.

This rule is intended to streamline administrative appellate review by the Board and will benefit aliens, including particularly vulnerable groups, by removing obstacles to timely adjudications. See 91 FR 5270. Moreover, this rule does not distinguish between individuals based on race, nationality, ethnicity, or any other protected characteristic. As detailed in the IFR, the Department is changing the regulations to provide the Board with more flexibility in reviewing appeals, allowing the Board to focus its limited resources on addressing the backlog of pending appeals and, going forward, ensure that aliens benefit from efficient adjudication of appeals.

In doing so, the Department considered the impact that the IFR would have on specific populations, including those highlighted by commenters above. See 91 FR 5270 n.9–10; id. at 5272 n.16; id. at 5273. The Department considered the potential effects of the IFR’s changes, including on the populations mentioned by commenters, but ultimately determined that the changes would provide significant benefits that outweigh the potential costs. See 91 FR 5276. The Department discusses the impact on those populations below; for a more detailed discussion of the specific provisions referenced by commenters and relevant due process and statutory concerns, please see Section III.C of this preamble.

The Department recognizes that pro se aliens can face difficulties while navigating the immigration system, as compared to those with counsel. See 91 FR 5272 n.16. These difficulties are to be expected with respect to any unrepresented individual in a legal setting. As a general matter, the Department notes the statutory right to self- funded counsel, see INA 240(b)(4)(A), 8 U.S.C. 1229a(b)(4)(A), and the ability to seek pro bono legal counsel.31 The Department also notes that many aliens voluntarily choose to forgo counsel for personal reasons and that commenters did not explain why those who deliberately choose to proceed without counsel should receive special solicitude. The IFR explicitly considered the impact on unrepresented aliens and their access to counsel. See 91 FR 5272 n.16. As explained in Section III.C of this preamble, the rule is entirely focused on the administrative appellate process and does not change any alien’s right or ability to obtain or confer with counsel when initially placed into removal proceedings or at any other point in time. And, in fact, the Department notes that a clear majority of aliens appearing before the Board have representation. For those who do not, various regulations implement an alien’s right to self-funded counsel and to seek pro bono counsel by requiring Immigration Judges to advise aliens of that right and the availability of pro bono legal services. See 8 CFR 1240.10(a)(1), (a)(2); see also 8 CFR 1003.61(b) (requiring the Director of EOIR to maintain the List of Pro Bono Legal Service Providers and update it not less than quarterly). The Department notes that aliens are entitled by statute to only 10 days to seek counsel before their case may proceed at the trial level, which mirrors the IFR’s 10-day appeal window. See INA 239(b)(1), 8 U.S.C. 1229(b)(1).

Furthermore, pro se aliens have the ability to request continuances to obtain counsel while in proceedings. Additionally, a pro se alien unable to obtain counsel prior to the deadline for filing a Notice of Appeal will have additional time to seek counsel if the Board accepts the appeal for consideration with briefing prior to filing a PFR with the Federal courts. See INA 242(b)(1), 8 U.S.C. 1252(b)(1). The Department, therefore, continues to anticipate that the rule would have any potential impact only on the relatively small number of pro se aliens who may not be able to find legal counsel, or 31 See, e.g., EOIR, PM 21–08, Pro Bono Legal Services (Dec. 10, 2020), https://www.justice.gov/eoir/book/file/1446651/download [https://perma.cc/U6ZW-FX8U]. secure limited document assistance, after diligent attempts to do so, in time to file a Notice of Appeal. Commenters did not provide evidence that this population of pro se aliens would be especially larger than the current number of unrepresented aliens before the Board,32 and having considered that impact, the Department finds it is outweighed by the efficiency benefits associated with the rule.

Separately, the Department finds that commenters were speculating as to the impact that the rule’s provisions will have on pro se aliens’ ability to adequately file a Notice of Appeal. Functionally, the change in the appeal deadline implemented by this rule is 20 fewer days to seek counsel in proceedings that often have taken years to complete. Nor are the filing or briefing deadlines impediments to effective representation. There is no reason that pro se aliens should be unable to file an adequate and timely Notice of Appeal identifying the relevant issues to be considered on appeal with the requisite specificity—just as pro se aliens do under the current regime. Contrary to commenters’ characterizations, there is no change in the IFR requiring that issues must be raised with a high level of exactitude. Rather, the Notice of Appeal must simply include enough specific information that the Board can review the issues being appealed and, under this rule’s procedures, determine whether to accept the appeal for further review with briefing. See Form EOIR-26, Notice of Appeal from a Decision of an Immigration Judge, Sec. 6, (Sept. 2019), https://www.justice.gov/eoir/file/eoir26/dl [https://perma.cc/P3PP-7T3H] (“State in detail the reasons for this appeal.”); see also Nolasco-Amaya, 14 F.4th at 1012 (an alien must “provide meaningful guidance to the BIA by informing it of the issues contested on appeal; a generalized and conclusory statement about the proceedings before the [Immigration Judge] does not suffice”) (cleaned up).

32 See generally EOIR, Current Representation Rates (Nov. 18, 2025), https://www.justice.gov/eoir/media/1344931/dl?inline [https://perma.cc/QC5J-3DD6]. With regard to commenters’ concerns about the availability of electronic filing for pro se aliens, the Department notes that the Respondent Access Portal allows for the electronic filing of the Notice of Appeal.

Although commenters expressed concerns regarding pro se aliens or new counsel having to file a Notice of Appeal without having access to the oral decision being challenged, the Department notes that, as discussed in Section III.C.2 of this preamble, when issuing a decision orally, the Immigration Judge must state the decision in the presence of the parties. See 8 CFR 1003.37(a). The alien, therefore, will be present for the issuance of an oral decision, and the Department is confident that Immigration Judges will clearly and adequately orally explain any basis for their decision, taking into consideration the circumstances of the alien. Aliens may then use that knowledge when preparing and submitting a Notice of Appeal.

The IFR further maintains Board discretion over briefing extensions and supplemental briefing. See 91 FR 5277. Further, as noted above, pro se aliens benefit from a statutory right to file a motion to reconsider an Immigration Judge’s decision to address “errors of law or fact in the previous order . . . .” See INA 240(c)(6), 8 U.S.C. 1229a(c)(6). In addition, exceptional situations may be addressed on a case-by-case basis through the Board’s consideration of equitable tolling.

Next, the Department has considered the potential that the rule—despite the safeguards just mentioned—may impact some pro se aliens’ ability to file their appeal or PFR as a result of the generally shortened Board appeal deadline, the comparative complexity of PFRs, and the lack of automatic stays of removal in Federal courts. Although commenters may prefer an automatic stay at the Board to a discretionary stay before the Federal courts,33 Congress, as discussed in Section III.C.1.a of the preamble, 33 Moreover, several circuit courts of appeals have local rules or practices under which the filing of a PFR and a timely stay motion does effectively trigger an automatic stay. See, e.g., National Immigration explicitly made such stays discretionary, see INA 242(b)(3)(B), 8 U.S.C. 1252(b)(3)(B), and this rule in no way affects Federal court adjudication of any such stay motions. Ultimately, the Department believes that the interest in timely adjudications outweighs these potential concerns.

The Department further acknowledges commenters’ concerns regarding the IFR’s impact on pro se detained aliens but does not believe that the rule makes it more challenging for pro se detained aliens to access legal representation or to file a timely appeal, as explained above with regards to pro se aliens more broadly. To the extent that commenters believe detained aliens should have improved access to counsel, faster communication, and better access to legal resources while in detention, those issues lie outside the scope of this rulemaking. The difficulties highlighted by commenters relate largely to challenges that existed prior to the IFR and by virtue of an alien’s detention or lack of representation, which remain unaffected by this rulemaking. Additionally, EOIR, DHS, and detained aliens, as well as the broader public, have a heightened interest in the efficient resolution of such cases, including any administrative appeals, given the potential liberty interests implicated when an alien is in detention during the pendency of a case before EOIR, as well as heightened costs to the Government. As such, it is even more important that a case involving a detained alien does not remain pending with the Board for longer than necessary. This rule’s provision for summary dismissal, except in those cases in which the Board has determined further briefing and administrative review is needed to address novel or complex situations, will help promote these policy interests. With regard to indigent or low-income aliens, this rule does not affect an alien’s ability to request fee waivers under existing regulations, as discussed in Section III.C.2 of this preamble. See 8 CFR 1003.8(a)(3). The Department emphasizes that the recent Litigation Alliance, Courts of Appeals Rules Governing Judicial Motions to Stay Removal, https://immigrationlitigation.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/01/2023.11-Circuit-Stay-Rules-FINAL- FINAL.pdf [https://perma.cc/7R93-JC4Y]. This rule does not affect those rules or practices. statutory changes in filing fees and the applicability of a waiver for certain fees are beyond the purview of the Department and beyond the scope of this rulemaking.34 Relatedly, the Department recognizes the categorization of UACs and the unique protections afforded them under the law, including in the TVPRA and within the immigration system. See, e.g.., INA 208(b)(3)(C), 8 U.S.C. 1158(b)(3)(C) (stating that an Asylum Officer has initial jurisdiction over the asylum claims of UACs); 8 U.S.C. 1232(d)(8) (“Applications for asylum and other forms of relief from removal in which a [UAC] is the principal applicant shall be governed by regulations which take into account the specialized needs of [UACs] and which address both procedural and substantive aspects of handling [UACs]’ cases.”); 8 U.S.C. 1232(c)(5) (TVPRA’s provision that “[t]he Secretary of Health and Human Services shall ensure, to the greatest extent practicable . . . that all unaccompanied alien children who are or have been in the custody of the Secretary or the Secretary of Homeland Security, and who are not described in subsection (a)(2)(A), have counsel to represent them in legal proceedings.”). The Department acknowledges that the Government is statutorily required to “ensure, to the greatest extent practicable” that UACs are represented in Immigration Court, though that does not categorically require access to counsel in every removal proceeding. See 8 U.S.C. 1232(c)(5). But the IFR is consistent with these laws and regulations, including the TVPRA; nothing in this rule is implicated by, or conflicts with, the provisions therein because those statutes and regulations do not relate to the Board’s appellate procedures. The Department recognizes commenters’ concerns that UACs may not have the autonomy or understanding of proceedings to assert their claims on appeal or to seek adequate representation, but these obstacles existed prior to the changes made by the IFR, and the existing protections that serve this population are intended to address such obstacles. Further, with respect to the effects of trauma on children and concerns about 34 See OBBBA, Pub. L. 119–21, sec. 100013(d)–(e), 139 Stat. 72 (2025).

re-traumatization, the Department is confident in the ability of Immigration Judges and the Board to follow appropriate safeguards available for children in processing appeals. Adjudicators receive training and guidance related to special considerations in cases involving children.35 The Board also has the ability to exercise discretion in extending deadlines and granting supplementary briefing to aid in accounting for these special considerations.

The Department additionally recognizes the difficulties faced by aliens with mental impairments, disabilities, and associated competency issues. However, this rule does not in any way alter existing protections for aliens with mental impairments and other competency issues. Notably, the Board’s decision in Matter of M-A-M-, 25 I&N Dec. 474 (BIA 2011), continues to provide applicable guidelines for assessment of competency issues in proceedings before EOIR. Furthermore, this rule in no way impacts existing programs like the National Qualified Representative Program (“NQRP”) for detained aliens who are found mentally incompetent.36 The Department believes that the existing protocols, in conjunction with the Board’s discretionary authority to extend filing deadlines in appropriate situations and the various exceptions provided by the rule, are sufficient to ensure fairness towards aliens with mental competency issues. The Department finds commenters’ assertions regarding victims of human trafficking facing difficulties in meeting the appeal deadline and the resulting loss of critical information that would help dismantle human trafficking networks to be highly speculative given the resources and protections in place for such individuals.37 35 See, e.g., EOIR PM 17–03: Guidelines for Immigration Court Cases Involving Juveniles, Including Unaccompanied Alien Children (Dec. 20, 2017), https://www.justice.gov/eoir/file/oppm17-03/download [https://perma.cc/J6LG-SHY6] (recognizing unique circumstances presented by immigration cases involving children and providing guidance for those cases); see also EOIR, Policy Manual, pt. II, ch. 3.21 (Feb. 10, 2026), https://www.justice.gov/eoir/policy-manual-eoir/part-II/icpm/chapter-3-21 [https://perma.cc/RS8P-YQ4A] (delineating safeguards for juvenile appearances in Immigration Court). 36 See EOIR, National Qualified Representative Program (July 23, 2025), https://www.justice.gov/eoir/ national-qualified-representative-program-nqrp [https://perma.cc/3F46-DJ95]. 37 See, e.g., EOIR PM 17–03: Guidelines for Immigration Court Cases Involving Juveniles, Including With respect to commenters’ concerns that low-literacy and non-English-speaking aliens may be impacted by the IFR’s changes due to the need to procure translations of documents and interpretation of communications, the Department notes that nothing in the IFR prevents an alien from coordinating with counsel, an interpreter, or a translator, if the alien chooses, as needed to pursue an appeal. To the extent the concern relates to the alien’s evidence, most commenters failed to acknowledge that all evidence submitted in an immigration hearing, regardless of who submits it, is to be submitted in English or with an English translation. See 8 CFR 1003.33. As such, evidence filed with the Immigration Courts that serves as the basis for appeal will already have a translation. Additionally, nothing in the statute or regulations requires that evidence of record be written or explained in the alien’s native language. Cf. Singh v. Holder, 749 F.3d 622, 626 (7th Cir. 2014) (“[I]n the immigration context, personal service in English to a non- English-speaker typically satisfies due process because it puts the alien on notice that further inquiry is needed, leaving the alien to seek help from someone who can overcome the language barrier.”); Ojeda-Calderon v. Holder, 726 F.3d 669, 675 (5th Cir. 2013) (“Due process allows notice of a hearing to be given solely in English to a non-English speaker if the notice would put a reasonable recipient on notice that further inquiry is required.”).

The Department also acknowledges that certain other populations may have unique vulnerabilities while navigating the immigration system. The Department notes that the rule and its exceptions apply equally to all aliens, regardless of nationality, race, ethnicity, or other demographics of concern identified by the commenters. Further, as explained in this section, adjudicators receive training to help them account for the harm that any particular alien, regardless of the alien’s group, may face. See EOIR, Fact Unaccompanied Alien Children (Dec. 20, 2017), https://www.justice.gov/eoir/file/oppm17-03/download [https://perma.cc/J6LG-SHY6] (delineating human trafficking protocols for EOIR); see INA 101(a)(15)(T)–(U), 8 U.S.C. 1101(a)(15)(T)–(U) (T and U visa provisions).

Sheet: Immigration Judge Training Fact Sheet (Aug. 2026), https://www.justice.gov/eoir/page/file/1513996/dl?inline [https://perma.cc/Q3AK-N7ZF]. Adjudicators can apply that training when exercising their discretion. As described above, the Board maintains the ability to exercise discretion in extending deadlines and granting supplementary briefing to account for special considerations on a case-by-case basis through the Board’s consideration of equitable tolling. The Board can also grant aliens additional time to seek counsel if the Board accepts an appeal for consideration with briefing prior to the alien filing a PFR with the Federal courts. See INA 242(b)(1), 8 U.S.C. 1252(b)(1). The Department also has confidence in the Board’s ability to follow all relevant laws and policies, described above, that aim to protect vulnerable groups. The Department further disagrees with commenters that it will be unclear which deadline applies to an asylum case because aliens will not know on what basis an Immigration Judge denied an asylum application. The Department is confident that Immigration Judges will clearly articulate any basis for denying an alien’s asylum application such that the applicable appeal-filing deadline will be readily apparent.
