Additionally, the Department expects that Immigration Judges will advise aliens of the applicable appeal deadline as part of the obligation to advise an alien of his or her appeal rights. See INA 240(c)(5), 8 U.S.C. 1229a(c)(5) (requiring the Immigration Judge, if ordering an alien removed, to “inform the alien of the right to appeal that decision”); 8 CFR 1240.10(a)(3) (requiring the Immigration Judge to “[a]scertain that the respondent has received a copy of appeal rights”); see also EOIR, Policy Manual, pt. II, ch. 3.15(h) (Feb. 10, 2026), https://www.justice.gov/eoir/policy-manual-eoir/part-II/icpm/chapter-3- 15 [https://perma.cc/HK27-PJAZ] (stating that “the Immigration Judge informs the parties of the deadline for filing an appeal with the Board, unless the right to appeal is waived”). The Department notes commenters’ concerns regarding the additional strain that the rule will potentially place on pro bono providers and organizations who serve pro se and indigent aliens. To the extent that commenters posited hypothetical scenarios about particular pro bono service providers, law student clinics, or particular types of cases, the Department notes that if such scenarios materialize in practice, then the Board can consider whether any of the factors referenced by the commenters warrant additional briefing or extensions. The intent of this rule is to streamline the appellate process and avoid undue delays. Because lengthy delays in immigration proceedings often dissuade pro bono representation, especially by law student clinic volunteers, ensuring expeditious adjudication of appeals may in fact encourage more pro bono representation.38 Further, nothing in this rule requires the diversion of resources or alteration of the mission of any low cost or pro bono legal service providers, including nonprofit organizations, pro bono volunteers, clinics and law students, and Government-funded representatives, beyond what is already required by existing regulations and professional responsibility requirements. For example, Immigration Judges already possess the authority to set shorter application filing deadlines. See 8 CFR 1003.31(h). Further, practitioners are already prohibited from taking on more work than they can handle competently. 8 CFR 1003.102(q)(1). Thus, pro bono organizations already operate under the conditions outlined in this rule. Although the Department acknowledges that nonprofit organizations, pro bono volunteers, and Government-funded representatives may prefer longer deadlines—as most legal representatives do, especially when additional delays benefit their clients—the Department is confident that such representatives will be able to handle such deadlines, just as they do in other courts and just as they handle all regulatory changes inherent across Government agencies, and will 38 Human Rights First, In the Balance: Backlogs Delay Protection in the U.S. Asylum and Immigration Court Systems (Apr. 2016) at 16, https://humanrightsfirst.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/11/HRF-In-The- Balance.pdf [https://perma.cc/8CV2-WB9R] (finding, based on a 2016 survey of pro bono coordinators, that “nearly 75 percent of pro bono professionals indicated that delays at the immigration court are a significant or very significant negative factor in their ability to accept a case.”), id. at 18 (finding that “[l]aw school clinics also report wasted resources and concerns about clients’ re-traumatization when they repeat their stories to new students.”); see also EOIR, PM 21-08, Pro Bono Legal Services (Dec. 10, 2020) at fn. 4, https://www.justice.gov/eoir/media/1387501/dl?inline [https://perma.cc/H53U-TE7X]. continue to be able to provide assistance and resources to aliens in proceedings before EOIR. It is not the Department’s responsibility to account for the staffing requirements, training, expertise, or opportunities for appearances of pro bono providers, organizations, and volunteers before the Board, in its rulemaking. Nevertheless, the Department has considered the concerns raised by commenters and has determined that they do not outweigh the benefits of this rulemaking.

Lastly, commenters made a number of recommendations regarding changes or alternatives to various provisions of the rule that, they suggested, would reduce the impact on the populations noted above, including a longer appeal deadline for aliens due to heightened burden in comparison with DHS, incorporating automatic extensions for detained aliens, acceptance of a “short form protective” Notice of Appeal followed by a supplemental statement of issues, and a “carve-out” for UACs and youth under the age of 21, requiring mandatory, non-discretionary further review with briefing in their appeals. The Department appreciates the recommendations submitted by commenters, but the Department has determined that none is preferable to the rule. In light of existing protections in place for these populations, the strong need to address the lengthy backlogs at the Board outweighs the interests advanced by commenters’ suggestions.

In short, the Department disagrees that the sorts of speculative challenges raised by the commenters are sufficient to outweigh the benefits obtained from this rule’s implementation. The IFR neither singles such aliens out for particularized treatment under the Board’s procedures, nor does it restrict or alter any of the avenues noted above that may assist pro se, detained, or otherwise vulnerable aliens. Further, the Department has difficulty responding to commenters’ generalized statements about various populations, trauma experienced by those populations, and other asserted difficulties because appeals are adjudicated on a case-by-case basis based on their specific facts. Given the limited available avenues for relief or protection and the risk of loss or degradation of evidence with the passage of time, the Department believes the significant efficiency benefits of the rule, on balance, far outweigh the speculative concerns raised by commenters. Moreover, in the event that there are “one-off” scenarios that do occur involving aliens in these groups, existing Board procedures—e.g., the use of equitable tolling—can address such situations on a case-by-case basis.

3. Rule Violates International Law Comment: Commenters argued that the IFR violates the United States’ obligations under international law because it violates aliens’ due process rights. Commenters also stated that the rule will have a discriminatory impact on aliens on the basis of national, ethnic, or social origin by limiting access to due process and appeals in Immigration Court, but not for non-Immigration Court matters. Commenters asserted that it would be a breach of international human rights obligations for the Department to subordinate equality and due process to its policy objectives.

Commenters also expressed concern that the IFR would exacerbate existing concerns about EOIR policies not complying with the United States’ international obligations against refoulement. Specifically, commenters said that the IFR’s provisions would prevent appropriate adjudications of claims for protection and limit meaningful appeal and review of asylum claims, thereby restricting access to asylum.

Commenters further expressed concern that the IFR precludes Board review of withholding-only proceedings. Commenters asserted that under the IFR, claims for both withholding of removal under section 241(b)(3) of the Act, 8 U.S.C. 1231(b)(3), and protection under the regulations implementing the CAT will be decided by Immigration Judges with no substantive appellate review available. Commenters cited Riley v. Bondi, 606 U.S. 259 (2025), in which the Supreme Court determined that the deadline to file a PFR for aliens in withholding-only proceedings is within 30 days of the prior removal order being reinstated. Thus, commenters stated, to obtain Federal court review in most withholding-only cases, an alien must file a PFR shortly after re-entering the United States or shortly after being arrested in the interior and having an old order reinstated. Commenters stated that most aliens are not able to locate counsel to file a PFR in that timeframe, and, in any event, until an alien has retained counsel, it is not logical to assume that they would wish to preserve their right to seek review of a withholding of removal or CAT decision before they have even filed for that protection (and in many instances before they have even received a reasonable fear interview placing their claims before an Immigration Judge).

Commenters noted that, under the IFR, the Board will continue to hear appeals in other matters where Federal court review is not available, including bond appeals and appeals of DHS visa decisions, but not withholding-only proceedings. Commenters argued that this prohibition on review does not make sense in the context of protection claims that are specifically designed to evaluate eligibility for mandatory forms of protection and comply with international human rights laws.

Response: This rule is consistent with international law, including the United States’ treaty obligations, and, as stated in Section III.C of this preamble, the Department does not believe that this rule violates due process rights in any way.

Three primary documents govern the rights of refugees and corresponding obligations of states in international law: the 1951 Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees, July 28, 1951, 19 U.S.T. 6259, 189 U.N.T.S. 150 (“Refugee Convention”); the 1967 Protocol Relating to the Status of Refugees, Jan. 31, 1967, 19 U.S.T. 6223, 606 U.N.T.S. 267 (“Refugee Protocol”), which incorporates Articles 2 through 34 of the Refugee Convention; and Article 3 of the CAT. Together, these documents provide a framework for states to provide protection to aliens fleeing persecution or torture and establish the principle of non-refoulement, which prohibits states from returning refugees to territories in specific circumstances.

These treaties, however, do not prescribe or impose any particular minimum procedures for implementation of non-refoulement obligations. Although the United States is a party to the Refugee Protocol39 and the CAT, these treaties are not directly enforceable in U.S. law. See INS v. Stevic, 467 U.S. 407, 428 & n.22 (1984); Al-Fara v. Gonzales, 404 F.3d 733, 743 (3d Cir. 2005) (“The 1967 Protocol is not self-executing, nor does it confer any rights beyond those granted by implementing domestic legislation.”); Omar v. McHugh, 646 F.3d 13, 17 (D.C. Cir. 2011) (explaining that the CAT “is non-self-executing and thus does not itself create any rights enforceable in U.S. courts”). Instead, the United States has implemented its obligations through domestic legislation and implementing regulations. The United States has implemented the non- refoulement provisions of the Refugee Convention through the withholding of removal provisions at section 241(b)(3) of the Act, 8 U.S.C. 1231(b)(3), rather than through the asylum provisions at section 208 of the Act, 8 U.S.C. 1158. See INS v. Cardoza- Fonseca, 480 U.S. 421, 429, 440–41 (1987).40 The United States has implemented its obligations under Article 3 of the CAT’s non-refoulement provisions through regulations. See Foreign Affairs Reform and Restructuring Act of 1998, Pub. L. 105-277, sec. 2242(b), 112 Stat. 2681–761, 2681–822 (codified at 8 U.S.C. 1231 note) (“FARRA”); see also, e.g., 8 CFR 208.16(c), 208.17, 208.18, 1208.16(c), 1208.17, 1208.18.

This rule does not change or limit ultimate eligibility for asylum, statutory 39 See Sale v. Haitian Ctrs. Council, Inc., 509 U.S. 155, 169 n.19 (1993) (“Although the United States is not a signatory to the [1951 Refugee] Convention itself, in 1968 it acceded to the United Nations Protocol Relating to the Status of Refugees, which bound the parties to comply with Articles 2 through 34 of the Convention as to persons who had become refugees because of events taking place after January 1, 1951.” (citation omitted)).

40As the Supreme Court explained, asylum “does not correspond to Article 33 of the [Refugee] Convention, but instead corresponds to Article 34[,]” which provides that contracting countries “shall as far as possible facilitate the assimilation and naturalization of refugees.” Cardoza-Fonseca, 480 U.S. at 441 (quoting Refugee Convention art. 34, 19 U.S.T. at 6276, 189 U.N.T.S. at 176); see also United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (“UNHCR”), Handbook on Procedures and Criteria for Determining Refugee Status and Guidelines on International Protection Under the 1951 Convention and the 1967 Protocol Relating to the Status of Refugees 16 para. 25 (2019 ed.) (“[T]he granting of asylum is not dealt with in the 1951 Convention or the 1967 Protocol”). Article 34 of the Refugee Convention “is precatory; it does not require the implementing authority actually to grant asylum to all those who are eligible.” Cardoza- Fonseca, 480 U.S. at 441.

withholding of removal, or CAT protection and accordingly does not implicate the United States’ non-refoulement obligations under international law. As explained in Section III.C of this preamble, none of the provisions contained in the IFR and adopted as final in this rule would prevent appropriate adjudication of claims for relief or protection, nor do they limit meaningful appeal or review of such claims. Instead, the rule is intended to reduce the backlog preventing such claims from being efficiently adjudicated. Furthermore, the rule does not violate the nondiscrimination requirement in Article 3 of the Refugee Convention, which prohibits discrimination on the basis of “race, religion or country of origin.” 19 U.S.T. at 6264, 189 U.N.T.S. at 156. As discussed in Section III.D.2 of this preamble, the rule does not discriminate on the basis of any of the protected characteristics described in Article 3. For the same reason, the rule does not violate other antidiscrimination principles described in other international human rights treaties, including the International Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination, arts. 2–5, Dec. 21, 1965, T.I.A.S. No. 94-1120, 660 U.N.T.S. 195 (signed and ratified by the United States), and the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, arts. 2–3, Dec. 16, 1966, T.I.A.S. No. 92-908, 999 U.N.T.S. 171 (signed and ratified with reservations, understandings, and declarations by the United States).

Neither is the rule inconsistent with Article 16 of the Refugee Convention or other international agreements to which the United States is a signatory. See Refugee Convention, art. 16, 189 U.N.T.S. 137 (Jul. 28, 1951). Article 16 of the Refugee Convention relates to access to courts, providing, in part, that refugees “shall have free access to the courts of law on the territory of all Contracting States.” Id. Commenters argued that the IFR imposes impediments on judicial review of EOIR decisions in the courts of appeals, thus impermissibly preventing refugees from freely accessing the courts. As discussed in Section III.C.1 of this preamble, however, the IFR’s summary dismissal procedures do not affect access to the courts of appeals. Rather, they affect only the Board’s review process, which is wholly within the authority of the Attorney General, as the Board is a regulatory creation of the Attorney General and its existence is not mandated by Congress. See Alexander-Mendoza, 55 F.4th at 197 (“An alien’s right to administratively appeal a removal order is not grounded in the Constitution.”); Dia, 353 F.3d at 242 (“Quite clearly, ‘[a]n alien has no constitutional right to any administrative appeal at all.’”).

Lastly, the Department disagrees with commenters’ assertions that the IFR’s summary dismissal provisions violate international law by further limiting substantive appellate review of statutory withholding of removal and protection under the CAT regulations in withholding-only proceedings, given the Supreme Court’s holdings in Riley. As relevant to Board appeals, nothing in this rule prevents an alien from filing a Board appeal in a relevant withholding-only proceeding. As explained in the IFR, the Department intended that the rule “would not change any existing understandings regarding when a removal order becomes final or when a petition for review must be filed.” See 91 FR 5271.

And regardless of how the Board chooses to handle a specific appeal, the alien will then maintain their existing ability to further file a PFR of that decision in the relevant Federal court. See, e.g., INA 242(b), 8 U.S.C. 1252(b) (providing requirements and standards for PFRs). Whether any timing issues regarding reinstatement of a prior removal order preclude such Federal court review is, however, outside the scope of this rule. In Riley, the Supreme Court recognized logistical concerns regarding when a removal order becomes final for purposes of Federal court review in withholding-only proceedings but ultimately determined the court “must nevertheless follow the statutory text and [] prior precedents.” 606 U.S. at 272.

E. APA Concerns Comment: Commenters raised APA concerns over the IFR’s justifications for foregoing standard notice and comment procedures, including concerns over the availability and duration of the comment period prior to the IFR’s issuance. Commenters argued that the APA’s procedural and foreign affairs exceptions did not apply to the IFR and that the Department’s invocation of these exceptions was improper. Commenters also stated that a regulatory flexibility analysis should have been conducted under the Regulatory Flexibility Act (“RFA”), specifically on the impact of the IFR on nonprofit organizations serving aliens in immigration proceedings.

Commenters claimed that the APA exceptions should be read narrowly, and that the IFR’s justifications interpreted these exceptions too broadly. Other commenters claimed that the IFR did not adequately address the consequences of the IFR’s changes on the accuracy, uniformity, and fairness of the Board’s decisions, nor consider less restrictive alternatives. Commenters likewise claimed that future Administrations would use the same justifications in rulemakings, which would have a negative effect on the quality of such rulemakings.
Separately, commenters stated that the original 30-day comment period was not sufficient for such a significant rule.

Response: Commenters’ concerns regarding APA procedures echo those raised in recent litigation over the IFR. See Amica, 822 F. Supp. 3d at 168. However, as explained in Section I.D of this preamble, the Department’s publication of this final rule addresses these procedural concerns. The IFR contained a request for comments, and the Department has fully considered and responded to such comments in this final rule. Thus, the APA’s notice and comment procedures have been fully satisfied. See Little Sisters, 591 U.S. at 682–86 (“Formal labels aside, the rules contained all of the elements of a notice of proposed rulemaking as required by the APA.”).

Further, as discussed at length in Sections III.B. and III.C of this preamble, the final rule has addressed concerns about its effect on the accuracy, uniformity, and fairness of the Board’s decisions and considered alternatives; thus, it has addressed those concerns as they pertain to the IFR. The Department also finds commenters’ concerns about applying similar APA exception-related justifications to other rulemakings to be outside the scope of this rulemaking; such concerns can and should be raised in response to those rulemakings, as applicable.

With regard to the comment period duration, the Department extended the comment period to include an additional 30-day period in addition to the original 30-day period. See 91 FR 9705. Thus, the Department has no concerns that the total 60-day period was insufficient. This view is supported by the more than 1,600 comments received, including dozens of lengthy, detailed comments from interested advocacy organizations.

Finally, with regard to commenters’ claims that the Department did not adequately address the IFR’s impact on accuracy, uniformity, and fairness of Board decisions, commenters’ concerns are vague and relate to aspects of the law outside the Department’s control. For example, commenters expressed concern that, beyond correcting errors in individual cases, the Board serves an important function to develop, clarify, and harmonize immigration law, and that increased Federal court involvement in review of such decisions will raise the likelihood of acute inter-circuit conflict. However, EOIR cannot control which decisions are subject to an alien’s choice to seek Federal court review, nor can it accurately predict how the different circuits will rule on issues as they percolate. Even so, the Board will continue to clarify and harmonize immigration law through precedential decisions in cases where the en banc Board determines that further review and clarification is necessary.

Comment: Commenters also claimed that the IFR is arbitrary and capricious under the APA because it failed to consider important impacts on affected populations. Commenters stated that the rule would place significant burdens on aliens and their counsel by shortening appeal timelines and reducing the availability of substantive Board decisions through summary dismissal and limiting briefing. Taken together, these changes would make it difficult to present fully developed arguments to the Board, would reduce the availability of counsel, and would have a particularly detrimental impact on vulnerable populations, such as detained aliens, among others.

Commenters also noted that the IFR’s changes were occurring in the context of other changes to the Immigration Court system, including increased fee amounts, recent Board decisions tightening standards for relief, and personnel changes at EOIR, among others, that, according to commenters, raised the risk of higher Immigration Judge error rates going uncorrected under the IFR’s provisions.

Response: In issuing this rule, the Department explicitly considered the various impacts the rule may have on interested parties. See 91 FR 5270 n.9 (“The Department has considered the potential impacts of these amendments individually and in context with the other amendments made by this rule on aliens and attorneys appearing before EOIR.”). The Department further discusses such impacts in Section III.D.2 of this preamble. The types of concerns raised by commenters are commonly raised in response to EOIR rulemakings, and the Department is adept in considering the effects of regulatory changes on affected populations. See, e.g., Securing the Border, 89 FR 81156 (Oct. 7, 2024) (addressing similar categories of commenters’ concerns, including concerns related to APA procedures, due process, effect on vulnerable populations, etc.). In this rulemaking, the Department ultimately determined that significant changes are needed to address the Board’s significant backlog, and these changes outweigh any potential negative effects on aliens and their counsel, among others.

The Department also believes that commenters overstated the effect of the changes in considering the potential burdens of the rule. Certainly, the summary dismissal procedures mark a significant revision to Board processes. However, the basic process remains the same: aliens may still file an appeal with the Board and, if that appeal is denied, the alien may file a PFR with the Federal courts or file a motion to reconsider. Far from foreclosing the ability to correct significant Immigration Judge errors, the summary dismissal procedures are intended simply to separate straightforward cases with no—or harmless or nonmaterial—errors from those which require more attention by the Board.

Likewise, a 10-day appeal period of course necessitates quicker action than a 30- day appeal period. But the 10-day appeal period simply applies to the filing of a Notice of Appeal, which focuses on providing a concise explanation of the basis for appeal. Thus, the Department determined that, on balance, the efficiency savings of shortening the appeal period outweighed the burdens on aliens and their counsel in meeting the shortened deadline. Moreover, the Department also ensured the rule applies prospectively to limit any potential effects on aliens and their counsel whose cases are currently in the appellate process. Accordingly, these changes should not undermine any reliance interests of either an alien or DHS. See 91 FR 5271 (“Because there is no right to a merits adjudication of any appeal in the first instance, and because the rule does not change the process for aliens who submitted an appeal with the expectation of receiving a different process, this change will not undermine any reliance interests of either an alien or DHS. Indeed, there is no evidence that DHS initiates a case in immigration proceedings or an alien brings a claim for relief or protection from removal based on the availability of an appeal to the Board if they lose, nor is there any logical reason that either party would do so.”) F. Miscellaneous Comment: Commenters claimed that the IFR would erode public confidence in the integrity of the immigration adjudication system and that the system is harmful and dehumanizing.

Response: The Department strongly disagrees with commenters. On the contrary, the Department believes that the full and efficient enforcement of the Nation’s immigration laws will inspire confidence in EOIR and the Immigration Court system. Undoubtedly, prior practices and poor agency management have undermined public confidence in EOIR and eroded the integrity of EOIR as an impartial adjudicatory agency.41 But the agency has recently made strides in restoring EOIR’s integrity as a preeminent administrative adjudicatory agency through the return of adjudicator impartiality and the rescission of policies unfounded in law. This final rule promotes efficiency in the agency’s appellate process and provides for prompt final determinations in immigration proceedings, thus taking another step toward reducing the backlog, enabling the prompt removal of aliens with no lawful basis to remain in the country, allowing for swifter corrections of Immigration Judge errors that result in wrongful removal orders, and strengthening public confidence in immigration decisions. See, e.g., Hernandez-Rodriguez v. Pasquarell, 118 F.3d 1034, 1042 (5th Cir. 1997) (citing Abudu v. INS, 485 U.S. 94, 106–08 (1988)) (“Both the public and the Board have significant, cognizable interests in the finality of immigration proceedings.”).

Comment: Commenters raised concerns about the IFR’s impact on public defenders advising their alien clients in State criminal court proceedings regarding the immigration consequences of criminal convictions. Specifically, commenters asserted that the IFR would significantly restrict the number of precedential decisions by the Board interpreting criminal statutes, which would in turn make it more difficult for attorneys to advise their alien clients regarding the immigration consequences resulting 41 See EOIR, PM 25-02, EOIR’s Core Policy Values (Jan. 27, 2025), https://www.justice.gov/eoir/media/1386541/dl?inline [https://perma.cc/LE74-NRTK]; EOIR, PM 25-04, Cancellation of Policy Memorandum 21-16 (Jan. 27, 2025), https://www.justice.gov/eoir/media/1386546/dl?inline [https://perma.cc/8ZLM-9H5X] (explaining management problems at the Board).

from a criminal conviction. Commenters also asserted that the IFR’s impact of expediting the removal of aliens would lead to even more unresolved State criminal cases where the alien is removed from the United States prior to resolution of the criminal matter. Commenters stated that the IFR may lead to inconsistent decisions among Immigration Judges regarding criminal issues and cited circuit splits between Federal courts interpreting the impact of criminal convictions.

Response: The Department does not expect that the streamlining measures adopted in this final rule will impact attorneys’ ability to advise alien clients regarding the immigration consequences of a criminal conviction. This rule in no way impacts or alters existing precedent from the Board or Federal courts nor materially alters the role that precedential authority plays in immigration proceedings. The Department further notes that one purpose of this rule is to free up resources to permit the Board to focus on cases presenting novel or complex legal issues—like, for example, novel criminal issues or interpretation of a criminal statute—which may lead to an increase in precedential decisions. See 91 FR 5271. This rule does not change any existing obligations attorneys have to their alien clients.

Regarding concerns related to inconsistent Immigration Judge decisions interpreting criminal statutes, those concerns exist under current procedures, and this final rule does not preclude the Board from reviewing such decisions and issuing a precedential decision to provide clarity and ensure consistent adjudications. In fact, the streamlining measures implemented in this rule will enable the Board to better focus its resources on issuing decisions to resolve such inconsistencies. Further, to the extent there are circuit splits on any issue, Immigration Judges and the Board are bound by the caselaw of each relevant Federal Circuit.
Comment: Commenters noted inconsistent Board appeal deadline language in EOIR’s Policy Manual.

Response: The Department is working to update all relevant EOIR materials related to changes made by this rule. To the extent that the Department has not yet updated any specific materials, the provisions of this rule supersede any such materials. Comment: Commenters alleged that the rule is inconsistent with 8 CFR 1003.1(a)(5), which states that en banc proceedings are “not favored.” Response: Although this rule is not inconsistent with the referenced regulatory section, which is focused on full en banc Board adjudications, the Department understands that the language may be confusing because the Board’s regular en banc process involves several steps. Accordingly, in response to the comment, and to avoid confusion, the Department is deleting the relevant language from 8 CFR 1003.1(a)(5). Comment: Commenters asserted that the IFR limited EOIR’s termination authority in most cases other than those involving UACs and questioned how this change improves efficiency.

Response: Commenters misunderstood the IFR’s changes to 8 CFR 1003.1(m)(2)(iii). The only changes made to that regulatory provision by the IFR and finalized in this rule are updating the term “unaccompanied children” to “unaccompanied alien children” and updating the cross-reference to the relevant statutory provision, 6 U.S.C. 279(g)(2), rather than a now-rescinded regulatory provision. Nothing in this rule changes termination authority.

Comment: Commenters noted that the IFR is silent on the Department’s obligations under the National Environmental Policy Act (“NEPA”). Commenters recommended that the Department add a categorical exclusion to its NEPA procedures to strengthen the legal foundation of the rule and bolster what commenters asserted is the Department’s position that the IFR does not require an environmental assessment. More broadly, commenters suggested that the Department could adopt a categorical exclusion for rules that do not increase immigration to the United States.

Response: The Department appreciates commenters’ suggestion related to establishing a categorical exclusion in Department NEPA procedures for rules that do not increase immigration to the United States. While outside the scope of this rulemaking, the Department will consider adopting such an exclusion to apply in future rulemakings to ensure compliance with NEPA when applicable.

Comment: Commenters recommended amending 8 CFR 1003.1(d)(6) to impose firmer deadlines for background-check-related requirements. Specifically, commenters suggested that an alien’s failure to comply with background-check requirements at the Board should be treated as automatically abandoning the underlying application for relief, absent a showing of good cause. Commenters stated that the good cause exception will ensure that aliens who face unusual or unpredictable hardships can proceed with their case while incentivizing aliens to comply with background-check requirements in a timely manner. According to commenters, this policy would be less likely to be abused than the existing policy at 8 CFR 1003.1(d)(6)(iii) authorizing the discretionary authority to continue holding cases.

Response: The Department declines to make the suggested changes to background-check procedures, which are outside the scope of this rulemaking. However, the Department may consider such a suggestion in a future rulemaking.

Comment: Commenters also proposed a number of alternatives to improve Board processing, including divesting the Board of jurisdiction to consider any appeal by DHS, any interlocutory appeal, any appeal of a bond decision, any appeal of the denial of a motion to reopen or motion to reconsider, and any appeal of the denial of a visa petition or nonimmigrant waiver. Commenters stated that the INA only requires an appeal as of right for aliens ordered removed, so the Department could eliminate all other types of appeals. Commenters noted that DHS could still request that Immigration Judges certify their decisions to the Board under 8 CFR 1003.7.

Commenters also suggested allowing aliens to waive preparation of a transcript if the Immigration Judge issued a written decision and a transcript would be unnecessary to resolve the appeal, stating this could avoid delays related to transcription. Commenters further suggested allowing aliens to consent to summary affirmance of an Immigration Judge’s decision if they intend only to raise challenges to the validity or constitutionality of a statute or regulation or arguments asking the Board to overturn a precedential Board decision.

Commenters also recommended requiring all motions to reopen to be filed with an Immigration Judge, regardless of the most recent decision on the merits, as Immigration Judges may be better suited to evaluate new or disputed factual claims. Commenters also suggested alternatives to benefit certain populations, including extending deadlines for underrepresented individuals and making notices more accessible and available in multiple languages.

Commenters suggested that the Department adopt performance metrics or reporting practices to evaluate the effectiveness of the new procedures adopted in this rule. Commenters recommended that metrics should consider timeliness, throughput, and indicators of adjudicatory quality, such as outcomes in subsequent judicial review, consistency across adjudicators, and reversal rates. According to commenters, transparency in reporting these metrics would enhance accountability and provide a basis for data-driven adjustments over time. Commenters also encouraged the Department to develop pathways for error correction in cases that present a higher risk of material error that may not initially be selected for consideration with briefing, such as an internal flagging system or review trigger. Commenters stated that the Department should commit to ongoing review of the rule’s implementation and effects to enable any necessary improvements should unintended consequences emerge.

Response: The Department appreciates suggestions to improve efficiency and streamline appeal processing and to evaluate the impact and effectiveness of this rule once implemented. The Department has considered these suggestions and determined that the streamlining measures adopted in this rule best address the efficiency needs at this time. Although the Department is declining to implement these suggestions as part of this rulemaking, most of which were beyond the scope of the IFR, the Department will continue to consider efficiency measures for adoption in potential future rulemakings, including those suggested by commenters. Further, although the Department declines to formally adopt any evaluative metrics as part of this rule, the Department will continue to assess the effectiveness of this rule as it is fully implemented.

IV. Statutory and Regulatory Requirements A. Administrative Procedure Act The Department is issuing this final rule after a 60-day notice and comment period, with full consideration of the over 1,600 comments provided, and a 30-day delay of the effective date. These procedures satisfy the requirements of the APA. See 5 U.S.C. 553(c)–(d).

B. Regulatory Flexibility Act Under the RFA, a regulatory flexibility analysis is not required when a rule is exempt from notice-and-comment procedures under 5 U.S.C. 553(b) or other law. See 5 U.S.C. 603(a), 604(a). To that end, the Department promulgated the IFR without prior notice and comment after determining the IFR related to agency procedure and involved a foreign affairs function, thus exempting the IFR from an RFA analysis under 5 U.S.C. 603 or 604. The Department continues to maintain the applicability of these exemptions to notice-and-comment procedures in promulgating the IFR.

However, even assuming that this rule is not exempt from notice-and-comment procedures and therefore not exempt from the requirements of the RFA, the Department has reviewed this rule in accordance with the RFA. The Acting Director of EOIR, under rulemaking authority delegated by the Attorney General, certifies that this rule will not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities. See 5 U.S.C. 605(b).

First, the rule regulates aliens, and aliens are not “small entit[ies]” as defined by the RFA. See 5 U.S.C. 601(6) (defining “small entity” as having the same meaning as “small business,” “small organization,” and “small government jurisdiction” as defined in 5 U.S.C. 601(3)–(5)). Second, to the extent that legal service organizations qualify as “small entities,” this rule does not directly regulate them and would not be expected to have a direct effect on them. Third, even if the rule does have an effect on legal services organizations, any economic effects of this rule on such organizations would not be significant under the RFA. The rule will not economically impact representatives of aliens in immigration proceedings. It does not limit the fees they may charge or the number of cases a representative may ethically accept under the rules of professional responsibility.

For example, this rule’s changes to summary dismissal procedures focus on which cases the Board chooses to accept for full briefing and further review, but does not affect the overarching process for filing an appeal itself. At the conclusion of proceedings before the Immigration Judge, aliens (or their counsel) will continue to file a Notice of Appeal with the Board, specifying the reasons for appeal and indicating whether they intend to file a brief at a later date. As such, no changes are required by the parties to comply with this new process.

Similarly, this rule’s changes to shorten the appeal period and to require simultaneous briefing without reply briefs will require legal service providers to adjust to these new timelines. However, the Department expects legal service organizations to quickly acclimate without substantial disruption, as the baseline process for filing an appeal remains the same and simultaneous briefing has long been standard for detained cases. Moreover, in non-detained cases, although parties have generally been granted 21 calendar days to file briefs, as stated in the IFR, the Board has long had the authority to set shorter briefing schedules at its discretion, 91 FR 5273 (citing 8 CFR 1003.3(c) (2023)), a possibility for which counsel should have already been prepared to accommodate prior to issuance of this IFR and final rule. The delayed effective date and prospective application of the IFR and this final rule, as well as delays caused by litigation, have also provided legal service organizations with further notice of and opportunity to prepare for these changes without substantial impacts to their current operations, including existing clients who have already filed their appeals. Thus, any costs incurred in adapting to the new timelines are not expected to be significant under the RFA.

Moreover, this rule does not limit or otherwise dictate the fees that legal service providers may charge or the number of cases the organization may ethically and competently accept. See Mid-Tex Elec. Co-op., Inc. v. FERC, 773 F.2d 327, 342–43 (D.C. Cir. 1985) (concluding “an agency may properly certify that no regulatory flexibility analysis is necessary when it determines that the rule will not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities that are subject to the requirements of the rule” and stating that legislative history of the RFA “gives rise to an inference that Congress did not intend to require that every agency consider every indirect effect that any regulation might have on small businesses in any stratum of the national economy”).

Finally, this approach is consistent with previous similar rulemakings regarding immigration regulations intended to regulate aliens and streamline immigration proceedings in which the Attorney General certified that such rule would not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities. See, e.g., Inspection and Expedited Removal of Aliens; Detention and Removal of Aliens; Conduct of Removal Proceedings; Asylum Procedures, 62 FR 444, 453 (Jan. 3, 1997) (certifying that the rule would not have a significant impact on a substantial number of small entities because it “affects only Federal government operations by codifying statutory amendments to the Immigration and Nationality Act primarily regarding the examination, detention, and removal of aliens from the United States” and did not impose reporting or compliance requirements on small entities).

In particular, this determination is consistent with the Department’s prior determination regarding much more sweeping changes to procedures before the Board. See 67 FR 54900 (“The Attorney General, in accordance with 5 U.S.C. 605(b), has reviewed this rule and, by approving it, certifies that it affects only Departmental employees, aliens, or their representatives who appear in proceedings before the Board of Immigration Appeals, and carriers who appeal decisions of [DHS] officers. Therefore, this rule does not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities.”). The Department is unaware of any challenge to that determination regarding its 2002 rulemaking which significantly streamlined Board operations and made much greater changes to Board procedures, including altering the Board’s standard of review for credibility determinations, than this final rule. The Department thus believes that the experience of implementing that prior, broader rule also supports its conclusion that there is no evidence that this final rule will have a significant impact on a substantial number of small entities as contemplated by the RFA.

The Department’s experience implementing these previous rulemakings further supports its analysis of this rule under the RFA and certification that the rule will not have a significant impact on a substantial number of small entities.

C. Unfunded Mandates Reform Act of 1995 This rule will not result in the expenditure by State, local, and Tribal governments, in the aggregate, or by the private sector, of $100 million or more in any one year (adjusted annually for inflation), and it will not significantly or uniquely affect small governments. Therefore, no actions were deemed necessary under the provisions of the Unfunded Mandates Reform Act of 1995. See 2 U.S.C. 1532(a).

D. Executive Order 12866 (Regulatory Planning and Review), Executive Order 13563 (Improving Regulation and Regulatory Review), and Executive Order 14192 (Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation) Executive Orders 12866 and 13563 direct agencies to assess the costs and benefits of available regulatory alternatives and, if regulation is necessary, to select regulatory approaches that maximize net benefits. The Office of Management and Budget has determined that this rule is significant under Executive Order 12866.

Overall, the Department believes this rule will provide significant benefits to adjudicators, parties before the Board, the U.S. immigration system overall, and the broader public, which outweigh the potential costs. For example, the rule’s procedural changes to Board practices are intended to better promote the efficient completion of removal proceedings. Such changes benefit both aliens with meritorious claims, who will obtain relief or protection faster, and DHS, which will be able to remove aliens with meritless claims more quickly. Combined, such changes provide significant benefits to the functioning of the country’s immigration system overall and to the public as a whole. The Department does not believe there are any apparent definitive costs of this rule. However, the Department fully considered the various potential costs raised by commenters in response to the IFR, including potential social and economic consequences if an increased number of aliens are removed. These costs include, for example, any potential costs to aliens ordered removed after not being able to file a Board appeal under this rule’s streamlined procedures, increased workload for attorneys due to a shortened Board appeal filing period, and increased filing fees associated with any increase in PFRs to the Federal courts.

The Department believes that concerns about these costs are speculative and lack a factual basis. However, even taking any proffered costs as legitimate, on balance, the Department continues to believe that the significant efficiency benefits associated with this rule outweigh the potential costs.

Regarding Executive Order 14192, this rule is a “regulation[] issued with respect to a[n] . . . immigration-related function of the United States” and is therefore exempt from the requirements of Executive Order 14192 under section 5(a) of that Order. E. Executive Order 14294 (Overcriminalization of Federal Regulations) When an agency promulgates regulations with criminal regulatory offenses that are potentially subject to criminal enforcement, Executive Order 14294 requires the agency to explicitly describe the conduct subject to criminal enforcement, the authorizing statutes, and the mens rea standard applicable to each element of those offenses. This rule does not create a criminal regulatory offense and so is exempt from Executive Order 14924’s requirements.

F. Executive Order 13132 (Federalism) This rule will not have substantial direct effects on the States, on the relationship between the Federal Government and the States, or on the distribution of power and responsibilities among the various levels of government. Thus, the Department has determined that this rule does not have sufficient federalism implications to warrant a federalism summary impact statement under section 6 of Executive Order 13132. G. Executive Order 12988 (Civil Justice Reform) This rule meets the applicable standards under sections 3(a) and 3(b)(2) of Executive Order 12988.

H. Paperwork Reduction Act This rule does not propose new or revisions to existing “collection[s] of information” as that term is defined under the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995, Pub. L. 104-13, 109 Stat. 163, 44 U.S.C. chapter 35), and its implementing regulations, 5 CFR part 1320. However, the Department notes that EOIR is making nonsubstantive changes to EOIR forms and form instructions to address the changes implemented by this rule. I. Congressional Review Act This rule is not a major rule as defined by section 804 of the Congressional Review Act. 5 U.S.C. 804. This rule will not result in an annual effect on the economy of $100 million or more; a major increase in costs or prices; or significant adverse effects on competition, employment, investment, productivity, innovation, or on the ability of United States-based enterprises to compete with foreign-based enterprises in domestic and export markets.

Accordingly, for the reasons stated in the preamble, and by the authority vested in the Director, Executive Office for Immigration Review, by Attorney General Order Number 6260-2025, the IFR amending 8 CFR parts 1003, 1208, and 1240 that was published at 91 FR 5267 on February 6, 2026, is adopted as final with the following changes:

The revisions read as follows:
§ 1003.1 Organization, jurisdiction, and powers of the Board of Immigration Appeals.

(4) * * * A temporary Board member shall have the authority of a Board member to adjudicate assigned cases, including summary dismissal authority pursuant to paragraph (d)(2) of this section, except that temporary Board members shall not have the authority to vote on any matter decided by the Board en banc. * * * * * * * *

(ii) Consideration by the Board—(A) Summary dismissal generally. Except for appeals pursuant to paragraphs (b)(5), (6), (7), and (14) of this section, and notwithstanding any other provision of this part (except for paragraph (d)(6) of this section), for all appeals of any decision issued on or after [INSERT DATE 30 DAYS AFTER DATE OF PUBLICATION IN THE FEDERAL REGISTER], the Board shall summarily dismiss the appeal without opinion unless a majority of the permanent Board members vote en banc to accept the appeal for further review after briefing. Nothing in this paragraph (d)(2)(ii) shall restrict the application of the provisions of paragraph (d)(2)(i) of this section or the authorities in paragraph (h) of this section.
